Examining Positive and Negative Affect as Outcomes and
Moderators of Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy and Acceptance and
Commitment Therapy for Social Anxiety Disorder
Amy R. Sewart ⁎
University of California, Los Angeles
Andrea N. Niles
San Francisco VAMedical Center
Lisa J. Burklund
University of California, Los Angeles
Darby E. Saxbe
University of Southern California
Matthew D. Lieberman
Michelle G. Craske
University of California, Los Angeles

Traditional cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) for anxiety
disorders has been designed to target reductions in negative
affect (NA) associated with defense-related processes.
However, a subset of anxiety disorders, including social
anxiety disorder (SAD), are also characterized by low
positive affect (PA) resulting from separate deficits in
appetitive-related processes. In contrast to CBT, “thirdwave” approaches, such as acceptance and commitment
therapy (ACT), align more consistently with motivational
processes and, as a result, PA. However, the differential
effect of CBT and ACT on PA and NA has yet to be
investigated. Using secondary data from a randomized
controlled trial, the present study sought to compare CBT’s
(n = 45) and ACT’s (n = 35) effect on PA and NA in SAD.
Findings were compared to a wait-list (WL) control

moderators and predictors of theory-relevant treatment
outcomes. NA decreased significantly in both CBT and
ACT from pre to posttreatment. Although ACT outperformed WL in reducing NA, this effect was not observed
for CBT. PA increased significantly in both CBT and ACT
from pre to posttreatment, with neither ACT nor CBT
outperforming WL in increasing PA. Neither PA nor NA
were found to moderate theoretically relevant treatment
outcomes. Findings suggest that ACT and CBT share
common treatment mechanisms, making them more similar
than distinct. Further efforts should be focused on optimizing CBT’s and ACT’s influence on threat and reward
learning, and elucidating common processes of change.

Keywords: social anxiety; cognitive-behavioral therapy; acceptance
and commitment therapy; positive affect; negative affect

ANXIETYDISORDERSHAVEBEENCHARACTERIZED by
behavioral inhibition, or the overactivation of a
proposed defensive system that serves to motivate

 sewart et al.
avoidance of perceived threats and aversive outcomes (Gray, 1994). The defensive system is posited
to generate certain forms of negative affect (NA)
that are a central feature of anxiety disorders, such
as fear and disgust (Davidson, 1994). In alignment
with this defensive system, “first-” and “secondwave” cognitive-behavioral approaches for anxiety
disorders almost exclusively focused on achieving
reductions in NA—including fear and anxiety—
and associated functional impairment (Barlow,
Ellard, Sauer-Zavala, Bullis, & Carl, 2014; Carl,
Soskin, Kerns, & Barlow, 2013; Craske, Meuret,
Ritz, Treanor, & Dour, 2016). For example,
exposure therapy works to lessen NA through a
mechanism principal to the defensive system: fear
extinction (Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek, &
Vervliet, 2014). Indeed, these strategies have
consistently demonstrated effectiveness in reducing
NA and related symptomatology (e.g., Craske et al.,
in press).
These traditional cognitive-behavioral approaches (referred to as “CBT”), however, have
largely disregarded positive affect (PA)—one’s
pleasurable engagement with the environment that
results in positive emotional states (e.g., joy,
interest, and enthusiasm)—an affective dimension
that is generated by a separate motivational system
related to appetitive and goal-directed behaviors
(Davidson, 1994, 1998). Deficits in PA are predictive and characteristic of certain anxiety disorders
(Khazanov & Ruscio, 2016; Kotov, Gamez,
Schmidt, & Watson, 2010), as well as depression
(e.g., Mineka, Watson, & Clark, 1998). CBTs have
not been found to significantly increase PA for
individuals with depression (g = .37, 95% CI [–
0.004, 0.77], p b .07; Boumparis, Karyotaki,
Kleiboer, Hofmann, & Cuijpers, 2016). Conceivably, CBT may also be insufficient for PA in
anxious individuals. Thus far, the effect of CBT
on PA for anxiety disorders has been examined in
only one study through person-specific analyses on
seven individuals with generalized anxiety disorder
(Bosley, Fisher, & Taylor, 2018). PA was found to
improve in only two of seven participants, and
worsened in five of seven—even as NA improved
over the course of treatment. Further investigation
of CBT’s effect on PA for anxiety disorders with
larger data sets is necessary.
Low PA appears to be particularly characteristic of
social anxiety disorder (SAD; Watson & NaragonGainey, 2010). A meta-analysis examining crosssectional and experience sampling studies found a
moderate, inverse relationship between social anxiety and PA, r = –.36, 95% CI [–.31, –.40], that
remained consistent after covarying for depressive
symptoms (r = –.21; 95% CI [–.16, –.26]; Kashdan,

1113

2007). These findings are paralleled with results
harnessing longitudinal datasets, experimental
designs, and structural equation modeling
methods (Brown, Chorpita, & Barlow, 1998;
Kashdan, Weeks, & Savostyanova, 2011; Khazanov & Ruscio, 2016; Sewart et al., 2019). Lack of
explicit attention to the positive dimension of
affect may in part explain less than optimal
treatment response rates for CBT for SAD (see
Loerinc et al., 2015).
The recent “third wave” in CBT has shifted away
from directly decreasing NA and instead focused on
acceptance and relinquishing control over maladaptive attempts to regulate internal mood states.
The third-wave movement has ushered in modalities that emphasize previously unaddressed concepts, such as mindfulness of the present moment,
acceptance of cognitions and feelings, and behaviors consistent with personal values (Hayes &
Hofmann, 2017). One of the most widespread of
these approaches is acceptance and commitment
therapy (ACT), which focuses on making contact
with the present moment and changing or persisting
in behavior to reach value-consistent goals, or
“psychological flexibility” (Hayes, Luoma, Bond,
Masuda, & Lillis, 2006). When compared with
CBT, ACT treatment philosophy aligns more
consistently with appetitive and goal-directed behaviors. For example, the core ACT process of
“committed action” requires engaging in activities
that align with personal values, which may serve to
recalibrate reward learning and increase positive
affective states, such as pride, gratitude, and
interest. Another core process of ACT, mindfulness,
is defined by (a) “the self-regulation of attention so
that it is maintained on immediate experience,
thereby allowing for increased recognition of
mental events in the present moment” and (b) “a
particular orientation toward one’s experiences in
the present moment, an orientation that is characterized by curiosity, openness, and acceptance”
(Bishop et al., 2004; Fletcher & Hayes, 2005).
While the goal of ACT is not to manipulate affective
states, heightened awareness of the present moment
may also serve to increase pleasurable engagement
with the environment and PA.
Given that CBT and ACT appear to target the
defensive and appetitive systems, respectively, it is
likely these therapies also possess differential
influence on PA and NA for SAD. Understanding
how currently disseminated treatments impact
affect and how baseline affect may predict treatment outcomes has high clinical utility, as such
knowledge may be used to guide treatment
planning. Furthermore, examining the effect of
CBT and ACT on both PA and NA contributes to

We first hypothesized that CBT would more
effectively decrease NA and symptoms when
compared with ACT. Further, CBT is expected to
be most effective for individuals with high NA,
given that the defensive system is the primary target
of CBT. Specifically, we hypothesized that reductions in NA would be greatest for individuals with
high NA receiving CBT compared to ACT. With
ACT strategies appearing to more directly target an
appetitive reward system, we hypothesized that
ACT would more effectively raise PA when
compared with CBT and that increases in PA
would be greatest for individuals with low PA
compared to CBT.
To investigate these hypotheses, we utilized an
existing data set to examine the main effects of CBT
and ACT on PA and NA. We compared these main
effects to a wait-list (WL) control condition to
better contextualize pre- to posttreatment gains.
Levels of PA and NA for each treatment condition
were then compared to a normative sample. Next,
we examined whether pretreatment levels of PA and
NA acted as moderators of treatment-relevant
outcomes for CBT and ACT, symptom reduction,
and quality of life, and resulted in differential
treatment response.

PARTICIPANTS

DESIGN

Participants who met criteria of the Diagnostic and
Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-IVTR; American Psychiatric Association, 2000) for
either principal or co-principal social phobia, generalized type, were randomly assigned and stratified by
age and gender to ACT, CBT, or WL. Using a
modified intent-to-treat approach, all participants
who began psychotherapeutic treatment and had
available data on variables of interest for at least one
time point (n = 111) were included in the present
analyses (n = 35 ACT, n = 45 CBT, n = 31 WL).
In addition to a diagnosis of generalized social
phobia, individuals were eligible for participation if
they were (a) between 18 and 60 years of age, (b)
either medication-free or stabilized on psychotropic
medication (i.e., 1 month for benzodiazepines and
beta blockers, and 3 months for selective serotonin
reuptake inhibitors [SSRIs]/serotonin–norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors [SNRIs] and heterocyclics),
(c) psychotherapy-free or stabilized on alternative
psychotherapies (not cognitive or behavioral therapies) that were not focused on their anxiety
disorder for at least 6 months, and (d) English
speaking. Exclusion criteria consisted of the following: (a) active suicidal ideation; (b) severe

TREATMENTS

Participants received 12 weekly, 1-hour individual
CBT or ACT therapy sessions by advanced clinical
psychology doctoral student therapists. Further
information regarding therapist competence, integrity, and training can be found in Craske, Niles, et
al. (2014). Treatment protocols used in each
condition were based on orientation-consistent
manuals (e.g., Eifert & Forsyth, 2005). Given that
both ACT and CBT focus to some extent on
avoidance reduction, treatments were matched on

Cognitive-Behavioral Therapy
CBT treatment modules for generalized SAD were
derived from standard CBT protocols (Hope,
Heimberg, & Turk, 2010). Session 1 was focused
on assessment, self-monitoring, and psychoeducation. Sessions 2–4 emphasized cognitive restructuring—specifically, errors of overestimation and
catastrophizing regarding negative evaluation—
these techniques were combined with strategies of
hypothesis testing, self-monitoring, and breathing
retraining. Rationale for exposure to socially
relevant feared cues was presented in Session 5.
Exposure—including in vivo, in vivo augmented
with interoceptive exposure, and imaginal—was
conducted in Sessions 6–11. Session 12 was focused
on relapse prevention.

PA and NA
In an effort to create a more valid and reliable index
of self-reported PA and NA, scores from two wellvalidated self-report measures were combined
following Z score transformation. PA was measured by the (a) positive affect subscale (PANAS-P;
10-item) of the Positive and Negative Affect
Schedule (PANAS; Watson, Clark, & Tellegen,
1988), a measure of dispositional affect in which
participants indicate the extent to which they felt
like a given affect-related adjective (e.g., “interested,” “distressed”) over the past week using a scale
from 1(very slightly/not at all) to 5 (extremely); and
(b) high positive emotion items from the anhedonic
depression subscale (MASQ-AD; 14-item; Kendall
et al., 2016) of the Mood and Anxiety Symptom
Questionnaire (MASQ; Watson & Clark, 1991) in
which participants are asked to rate the strength of
emotional experiences over the past week from 1
(not at all) to 5 (extremely). NA was measured by
the (a) negative affect subscale (PANAS-N; 10-item)
of the PANAS and (b) the general distress mixed
subscale (MASQ-GDM; 15-item) of the MASQ.
The PANAS and MASQ have been used frequently
in socially anxious samples (see Kashdan, 2007, for
a review) and across disorders to assess affective
abnormalities (e.g., Brown et al., 1998; Sewart et
al., 2019; Watson & Naragon-Gainey, 2010).
These measures have also demonstrated both
validity and good-to-excellent reliability in clinical
and nonclinical populations (Crawford & Henry,
2004; Jolly, Dyck, Kramer, & Wherry, 1994;
Keogh & Reidy, 2000; Mehrabian, 1997; Roesch,
1998; Watson, Clark, & Tellegen, 1988).

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy
ACT treatment modules for generalized social
phobia were developed largely from Eifert and
Forsyth (2005). Session 1 was focused on psychoeducation and orientation to ACT, which included
experiential exercises (e.g., “finger trap”) and a
discussion of acceptance and committed action.
Sessions 2–3 centered on creative hopelessness and
how attempts to control anxiety resulted in a
reduction of valued life activities; accepting anxiety,
rather than efforts to reduce, was encouraged.
Sessions 4–5 directed participants in practices of
mindfulness and cognitive defusion, while continuing to emphasize acceptance of anxiety. Sessions 6–
11 largely focused on values identification and
acceptance, with an additional component focusing
on continued practice of acceptance, mindfulness,
and defusion. When relevant, exposure—including
in vivo, in vivo augmented with interoceptive
exposure, and imaginal—was conducted in an
effort to have participants practice mindfully
observing and accepting anxiety while conducting
values-consistent action. Session 12 was focused on
what practices were helpful and how to continue
moving forward after therapy has concluded.

Quality of Life
The Quality of Life Inventory (QOLI; Frisch, 1994)
was used to assess QOL, an outcome that
corresponds with the overall goals of psychological
flexibility and valued living within ACT. The QOLI
assesses well-being and satisfaction with life across
16 domains (e.g., goals and values, friendships,
health). This measure has demonstrated good
internal validity and test–retest reliability (Frisch
et al., 2005).
STATISTICALANALYSES

Analyses were performed in Stata 14.0 using the
xtmixed command. We used multilevel modeling
(MLM), a superior statistical approach for data
with nested sources of variability, as it allows for
examination of within- and between-subject change
across time (pre, post, 6MFU, 12MFU) and by
group (ACT, CBT, and WL). MLM accommodates
unequal observations across individuals, allowing
for the inclusion of participants missing one or
more assessments.

Main Effects
For the main effect of treatment on PA and NA,
time was modeled at Level 1 (pre, post, 6MFU,
12MFU) using a piecewise approach (e.g., RoyByrne et al., 2005) that examines two separate
linear segments of change: Pre and post (S1) and
post, 6MFU, and 12MFU (S2). This approach
captures typical trends in treatment studies, wherein the greatest effect of treatment occurs by the end
of treatment and is then subsequently maintained,
or lessened, during follow-up assessments. Treatment group (CBT, ACT, and WL) was included at
Level 2. All models included random effects of the
intercept. Between-group differences were assessed
via marginal means at each time point, and by
comparing S1 in ACT, CBT, and WL, and S2 in
ACT and CBT. The MLM equation for a model
with random effects for the intercept can be
referenced in Craske, Niles, et al. (2014).
Moderated Effects
To examine the moderating effects of baseline PA
and NA on theory-relevant outcomes for ACT and
CBT, time was modeled at Level 1 and condition and
moderators at Level 2. Using a similar statistical
approach as the main effects, we examined pretreatment to posttreatment and posttreatment to followup as two separate linear segments as described
above. Separate moderator models were run for PA
and NA. Omnibus three-way interaction effects were
tested first (i.e., Time × Condition × Moderator). If
moderation was not observed, we followed up with
further testing to determine whether PA and NA
functioned as a nonspecific predictor of treatment
response to both CBT and ACT.

Results
Means and standard deviations of PA and NA,
along with theory-relevant outcomes examined in
moderator analyses are presented in Table 1. No
significant pretreatment group differences were
found between CBT, ACT, and WL for variables
of interest (ps N .23).
PAANDNAASOUTCOMEVARIABLES

Changes in PA and NA were examined by
determining whether each slope differed significantly from zero from pre- to posttreatment (S1)
for CBT, ACT, and WL and from 6MFU to
12MFU (S2) for CBT and ACT. Degree of slope
change in these segments was then compared
between groups. For Group × Time interactions,
we present beta values for pairwise slope comparisons (i.e., simple effects) and associated p
values. Estimated means and 95% CI from the
piecewise model for each group are displayed in

Table 2. Estimated slopes and effect sizes for
pairwise group slope comparisons are further
detailed in Table 3. Results are visually displayed
in Figure 1.
Negative Affect
From pre- to posttreatment (S1), NA decreased
significantly for both CBT (b = –0.5, 95% CI [–0.8,
–0.3], p b. 001) and ACT (b = –0.7, 95% CI [–0.9, –
0.3], p b. 001), but not WL (b = –0.2, 95% CI [–0.5,
–0.1], p = .18). For S1 pairwise slope comparisons,
ACT demonstrated larger reductions in NA than
WL (b = –0.5, 95% CI [–0.9, –0.1], p = .01). CBT,
however, did not outperform WL in reducing NA,
although the observed effect approached significance (b = 0.3, 95% CI [–0.04, 0.7], p = .08).
Inconsistent with our hypothesis, CBT and ACTS1
slopes did not significantly differ from each other
(b = –0.2, 95% CI [–0.5, 0.2], p = .39). S2 change
slopes were not significant in CBT (p = .19) or ACT
(p = .37).

Discussion
Anxiety disorders have long been characterized by
abnormal activation of a theorized defensive system
that gives rise to elevated levels of NA (e.g., fear;
Gray, 1994). As such, traditional CBT for anxiety
disorders has been designed to target reductions in
NA associated with defense-related mechanisms.
However, a subset of anxiety disorders, including
SAD, are also characterized by low PA resulting
from separate deficits in appetitive learning processes (e.g., Brown et al., 1998). In contrast to CBT,
“third-wave” approaches, such as ACT, have
focused on new treatment targets that—although
not a direct goal of these treatments—align more
consistently with and facilitate appetitive and goaldirected behaviors and, as a result, PA. However,
whether or not these treatment approaches actually
exercise differential influence on appetitive and
defensive systems has yet to be investigated. Thus,
using secondary data from a previously conducted
randomized controlled trial, the present study
sought to compare CBT’s and ACT’s effect on PA
and NA in SAD. The findings were compared to a
WL control condition, as well as normative data
from a general adult sample. In addition, we sought
to investigate baseline PA and NA as moderators
and predictors of theory-relevant treatment outcomes.
The present study has several main findings,
some of which contrast with our initial hypotheses.
First, NA decreased significantly in both CBT and
ACT from pre- to posttreatment with these
reductions maintained through follow-up assessments. However, contrary to our hypothesis, CBT
was not found to outperform ACT in decreasing
NA pre- to posttreatment. Moreover, whereas ACT
outperformed WL in reducing NA, the difference in
slopes between CBT and WL only approached
significance (p = .08). Comparing posttreatment

NA to population average data, as reported in one
reference study comprising an adult sample collected through various commercial and public service
organizations, levels of NA approached normative
values for CBT and ACT. Second, PA increased
significantly in both ACT and CBT from pre- to
posttreatment with these elevations maintained
through follow-up assessments and approaching
normative values for CBT and ACT. Again,
contrary to our hypothesis, ACT was not found
to significantly outperform CBT in increasing PA
pre- to posttreatment. Neither ACT nor CBT were
found to outperform WL in elevating PA pre- to
posttreatment. Third, pretreatment levels of neither
PA nor NA were found to moderate theoretically
relevant treatment outcomes for either CBT or
ACT.
In contrast with our hypothesized differential
moderation, pretreatment levels of PA functioned
as a nonspecific predictor of QOL in both ACT and
CBT. While individuals with low to average levels
of pretreatment PA experienced significant improvements in QOL, individuals with high pretreatment PA did not. As displayed in Figure 2, this
appears to be a ceiling effect due to individuals with
high pretreatment PA reporting high levels of QOL
prior to initiation of ACT and CBT, thus giving less
potential for improvement. These results may be
further explained by the “broaden-and-build”
theory of positive emotion, wherein positive emotions enhance QOL through encouraging enduring
personal resources and relationships and promoting exploratory and novel thoughts and actions—
thus broadening one’s behavioral range (Fredrickson, 1998, 2004). Overall, our PA predictor
findings corroborate a larger body of literature
that implicates PA as a significant, positive predictor of various QOL dimensions (e.g., Brennan,
Singh, Spencer, & Roberts-Thomson, 2006;
Headey, Kelley, & Wearing, 1993; Louro, Fernández-Castro, & Blasco, 2015; Stauber et al., 2013)
and highlights the importance of further identifying
psychotherapeutic strategies that more effectively
increase PA.
One of the most notable findings is that although
CBT significantly decreased NA pre- to posttreatment, this effect was not found to differ from WL.
There may be a number of explanations. One
possibility is that the treatment strategies (e.g.,
cognitive restructuring, exposure, and breathing
retraining) targeted specific threat responses (e.g.,
fears of specific stimuli) without influencing general
negative emotions.
Furthermore, while ACT and CBT were not
observed to exercise a differential effect on NA,
ACT did outperform WL with a moderate effect

 sewart et al.
size (d = 0.5). Although reducing NA is not a focus
of ACT, it is likely that this reduction is a byproduct of ACT-based strategies. For example,
carrying out committed action for an individual
with SAD may include spending more time
socializing with friends, which may serve to lessen
negative emotions. Why ACT outperformed WL
and CBT did not, is unclear. Based on these
contradictory findings, further research is needed
to examine changes in threat-related processes as a
result of CBT and ACT for anxiety disorders.
Another striking finding is that while ACT and
CBT significantly increased PA, neither treatment
outperformed WL pre- to posttreatment. This
converges with previous findings that cognitivebehavioral and mindfulness-based psychotherapies
are largely ineffective in heightening PA for
depression (Boumparis et al., 2016; Dichter et al.,
2009; Moore et al., 2013). Our results should be
interpreted with the acknowledgment that CBT for
SAD is not designed to target appetitive and goaldirected learning in the same manner as CBT for
depression. This is not to say that strategies in CBT
for SAD (e.g., exposure) should not also serve to
indirectly increase PA through encouraging contact
with feared situations that are likely to also be
rewarding (e.g., social gatherings). ACT, however,
seeks to improve QOL—a construct inherently
related to reward attainment—and yet it does not
outperform WL in increasing PA. These findings
call for clinical scientists to identify psychotherapeutic strategies that more effectively target the
appetitive approach system and—as a result—
increase PA for anxiety disorders that demonstrate
deficits, such as SAD and generalized anxiety
disorder (Prenoveau et al., 2010). As with NA,
further research is needed to examine changes in in
reward-related processes as a result of CBT and
ACT for anxiety disorders.
These results corroborate and extend our initial
outcome and moderator findings (Craske, Niles, et
al., 2014). Comorbid depression previously failed
to predict composite symptoms, which is consistent
with our PA finding given that low PA is
characteristic of depression (Watson, Clark, &
Carey, 1988). Craske, Niles, et al. (2014) found
extraversion to be a nonspecific significant linear
predictor of composite symptoms (z = 1.96, p =
.05), wherein participants higher in extraversion
reported significantly fewer symptoms collapsed
across follow-up assessments (Craske, Niles, et al.,
2014). There is both self-report and psychophysiological evidence to suggest that PA forms the
“conceptual core” of extraversion (Hermes, Hagemann, Naumann, & Walter, 2011; Lucas & Baird,
2004; Watson & Clark, 1997). This finding

1121

diverges from our current analyses that found that
pretreatment PA was neither a moderator nor a
nonspecific predictor of symptom reduction. One
potential explanation for these differing findings is
that extraversion is a socially relevant trait, whereas
PA encompasses more pleasurable engagement
broadly. The ability to derive positive emotional
states from social experiences may be particularly
beneficial for enhancing treatment response to both
CBT and ACT for individuals with SAD. Future
research should investigate the dynamics between
PA and social interaction in SAD and how their
relationship may affect treatment outcome.
As the field moves more toward a dimensional
understanding of psychopathology, it is essential
that we begin to examine our standard psychotherapeutic treatments from this perspective (Brown &
Barlow, 2009; Insel et al., 2010). This is the first
study to our knowledge that examines changes in
PA and NA as a result of CBT and ACT for anxiety
disorders. Our findings raise important questions
regarding the effectiveness of these interventions
with respect to defense and reward systems.
Furthermore, our findings suggest that individuals
with low PA may benefit from augmenting CBT
and ACT with strategies specifically designed to
regulate positive emotion. For example, individuals
with low PA may benefit from adjunctive training
in how to “savor” past, current, or future positive
experiences (Bryant, 2003) or “capitalize” on
success (Carl et al., 2013; Langston, 1994). Indeed,
protocols with such strategies have recently been
shown to significantly improve PA, although results
were not compared to WL (e.g., Craske et al., in
press).
Our study possessed some limitations. Given that
these two therapeutic approaches focus on avoidance reduction, exposure was employed in both
treatment conditions for an equal number of
sessions with an orientation-consistent rationale.
As a result, it is possible that exposure may be
driving effects in both ACT and CBT, making the
differential impact of these approaches less detectable and more difficult to assess—or less present
than suspected. Optimizing QOL is also a focus of
CBT that has more recently been examined as a
critical outcome of treatment success (e.g.,
Hofmann, Wu, & Boettcher, 2014). As a result,
contending that QOL is not theoretically relevant to
CBT as well is debatable. Given that PA and NA
were not assessed throughout treatment, we were
unable to examine these factors through mediational analyses that may have provided further
insight into the mechanistic nature of threat and
reward-related processes in CBT and ACT. Participants were deemed ineligible if they presented with

 1122

positive and negative affect as outcomes and moderators

severe depression (CSR ≥ 6 on a 0- to 8-point scale;
Brown et al., 1994). While this is not an uncommon
procedure for anxiety psychotherapy studies, this
likely excluded individuals with anhedonia and as a
result may have indirectly affected our PA findings.
To further examine treatment change, we compared levels of PA and NA to a nonclinical sample
collected in the United Kingdom with a mean age
(M = 42.9) and demographic composition that was
substantially different from our sample. Thus, these
normative values do not generalize to our sample in
an ideal manner. Last, we relied on self-report
measures as the exclusive modality of treatment
response, which may have inflated ratings (Loerinc
et al., 2015). However, our treatment’s main effects
more often than not did not outperform WL. Future
studies may address this limitation by employing
experimental paradigms that more directly measure
change in purported reward and threat-learning
mechanisms during treatment.
Overall, these findings suggest that while ACT
and CBT may approach psychotherapeutic treatment with different methods, they share common
treatment mechanisms making them more similar
than distinct. Still further research is needed to
elucidate common processes of change in CBT and
ACT. Future research should assess PA and NA
during CBT and ACT for a more rigorous
examination of these factors as potential mechanisms. Most importantly, efforts should be focused
on enhancing CBT’s and ACT’s influence on threat
and reward learning in an effort to better recalibrate PA and NA.

ABSTRACT

Keywords:
Social anxiety disorder
Social phobia
Acceptance and commitment therapy
Cognitive-behavioral interventions

Background: Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) or Social Phobia is characterized by fear and anxiety of social cir­
cumstances that negatively impact an individual's occupational and relational life. There are several treatment
options for this disorder ranging from pharmacological therapy to psychotherapies. In particular, the Acceptance
and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a form of cognitive-behavioral therapy that practices acceptance and aware­
ness strategies with behavior change strategies in order to increase an individual's mental flexibility, has been
found to be effective. In this review, we aimed to provide an overview of recent studies that examined ACT's
efficacy in SAD, also taking into consideration the comparison with traditional Cognitive-behavioral Therapy
(CBT) interventions.
Methods: A bibliographic search on PubMed, EMBASE and Scopus was conducted from inception to the 3rd of
February 2022 of all studies investigating the effect of ACT in SAD individuals without any comorbidity. Among
the articles retrieved, 11 met the inclusion criteria.
Results: From the reviewed studies, ACT may be considered a promising treatment of social phobia by improving
attentional bias, awareness, emotion regulation, and safety/avoidance behaviors; however, the results have not
yet demonstrated a valid alternative to the CBT.
Limitations: Only four studies considered a follow-up evaluation, which is paramount to exploring the effec­
tiveness of ACT and several studies have a very small sample size. Concerning the review itself we only
considered original English articles and we did not measure the risk of publication bias and the risk of bias
between studies.
Conclusions: The results of this study suggest that ACT can be a promising treatment for improving selective
psychological problems often observed in SAD. However, larger longitudinal studies further exploring the
effectiveness of the behavioral and cognitive “third-wave” psychotherapies, based mainly on acceptance of SAD,
are necessary.

1. Introduction
Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), also known as social phobia, is a
psychiatric disorder characterized by an intensive fear of being judged
by others or through experiencing embarrassing moments during
interpersonal interactions (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
SAD could be defined as a multifactorial disorder whose manifestation is
due to a complex interaction between gene and environment (Nagata,

2015); in addition, temperamental traits, which include behavioral in­
hibition and the fear of others' negative evaluation, may predispose to
the disorder (Rose and Tadi, 2021). Importantly, SAD has a very early
onset, with many cases beginning in childhood or early adolescence
(Chavira and Stein, 2005), and it may persist to adulthood and even old
age. As a result, it is commonly seen in primary care patients (Kroenke
et al., 2007). In SAD patients, the undesirable and disproportionate
evaluation of social situations intensifies anxiety (e.g., panic attacks,

such situations that are perceived to be threatening. These behaviors
lead to very limited and poor quality of life by increasing the difficulty in
creating positive events and memories and being part of emotional and
affective experiences (Kashdan et al., 2006).
The most common and effective pharmacological treatment is
identified in a class of drugs that are typically used as antidepressants,
the Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitors (SSRIs). Among nonpharmacological treatments, the Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
is considered as the first-line treatment by the National Institute for
Health and Care Excellence (National Institute for Health and Care
Excellence (NICE), 2013). It has been proven that the CBT teaches pa­
tients the cognitive and behavioral competencies needed to have an
adaptive behavior in their interpersonal and intrapersonal realities. It is
the best intervention for the initial treatment of SAD (Mayo-Wilson
et al., 2014), mainly due to the long-term beneficial effects observed
(Stein and Stein, 2008). The major CBT programs, which have demon­
strated their efficacy in controlled research for the treatment of SAD,
have applied exposure, cognitive restructuring, relaxation training, and
social skills training (Heimberg, 2002; Cuijpers et al., 2016; Evans et al.,
2021).
Furthermore, recent literature (Dimidjian et al., 2016; Feliu-Soler
et al., 2018) suggests that there might be new innovative forms of CBT,
which did not have first-order change as their only objective, but used
experiential and indirect change techniques besides direct strategies.
These are defined as “third wave” CBT therapies, which include the
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) (Hayes, 2004), the
Compassion-focused Therapy (Gilbert, 2010), the Mindfulness-Based
Cognitive Therapy (Segal et al., 2002), the Mindfulness-Based Relapse
Prevention (MBRP; Bowen et al., 2011), and the Mindfulness-Based
Eating Awareness Training (MB-EAT; Kristeller, 2019).
The pillars of the ACT approach are the “acceptance” and “defusion”
from self-thoughts and awareness of one's values, which go towards
comprehending what is happening in the present (Harris, 2016). This
aspect has become an object of interest for many clinicians (Hayes et al.,
2011) with preliminary investigations reporting its effectiveness in the
treatment of SAD (Azadeh et al., 2016; Clarke et al., 2020). In fact, the
purpose of this therapy is to help in distancing ourselves, realizing, and
understanding messages, as well as freeing ourselves from all those
thoughts and stories that our mind tells us (Hayes et al., 2012) rather
than repairing and modifying disturbing symptoms. In summary, the
strengths of ACT are its ability to a) deal with symptoms' perception and
discomfort, b) learn the necessary techniques to reduce not only the
struggles but the unnecessary avoidance of what hurts (especially
emotions), and c) eliminate the disconnection from the present moment
through the insertion of the concept of “flexibility” (Hayes et al., 2006).
ACT involves six specific psychological processes (Luoma et al., 2007):
a) the “cognitive defusion”, a skill used to take a distance from thoughts
without merging with them; b) the “extension”, which is used to create
space between emotions and unpleasant sensations; c) the consideration
of “self as a context” that changes the ability to observe the situation in
which the person is inserted; d) the “being present”, which represents
the idea making contact with the present moment; e) the concept
“values” that refers to an act that can be instantiated, moment by
moment, thus becoming the only compass to guide the action, and lastly,
f) the “committed action”: this is based on values, intentional and
motivational, that the individual should have without looking at fail­
ures. Accordingly, the first expected outcome of therapy based on the
emotions' acceptance, is the reduction of negative thoughts and a
consequent proactive and effective behavior rather than anxious
avoidance reaction to worrisome situations. Specifically for SAD, ACT
has proven to be useful in ameliorating social experiences by decreasing
the main symptoms of social anxiety and by increasing the willingness to
engage in social and/or performance situations (Block and Wulfert,
2000; Kocovski et al., 2009; Ossman et al., 2006).

2. Methods
The present review was performed according to the Preferred
Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)
guidelines and flow diagram (Moher et al., 2009). A comprehensive
search of all the studies using ACT in SAD patients, with no chrono­
logical limits and pre-specified restrictions (e.g., ethnicity) was carried
out in PubMed, EMBASE, and Scopus, using two separate strings of
keywords: “Acceptance and commitment therapy AND social anxiety
disorder” and “Acceptance and commitment therapy AND social
phobia”. The last investigation was conducted on the 3rd of February
2022. Concerning the eligibility criteria, we included all studies with
participants who had been formally diagnosed with SAD in accordance
with the definition of the American Psychiatric Association, through a
diagnostic interview, regardless of age. We also included subjects with
significant SAD symptoms, as measured with empirically validated
clinical scales. Participants were not expected to have comorbidities
with other anxiety/depressive disorders or substance dependence. Any
psychological intervention based on ACT in the form of either individual
or group interventions and studies with or without a control group were
included (i.e., waitlist, CBT both in individual and group form, cognitive
restructuring with exposure, only in vivo Exposure). All studies were
included if they had as primary outcomes the reduction of anxiety
symptoms, changes in the avoidance of situations and behaviors,
emotional reactivity and regulation, negative affect, psychological
flexibility and interpersonal problems. With regards to the study design,
we included either randomized/semi-randomized or non-randomized
clinical trials. Any setting or follow-up period was considered. Only
studies published in English were included. We excluded articles if they
were 1) reviews, meta-analysis, and publications different from original
articles (e.g., letter, book chapter, conference abstract); 2) validation
studies; 3) neuroimaging studies; 4) clinical trials with psychodynamic
or self-support therapies and 5) qualitative studies.
A manual selection of papers using headings and abstracts was per­
formed by three independent operators (C.M, E.C, and S.M.), with dis­
agreements resolved by the intervention of another reviewer (G.D).
Indeed, some disagreements emerged concerning studies that included
group-based ACT therapies or that were focused on performance anxiety
(i.e., public speaking anxiety and music performance anxiety). However,
a consensus was reached and all these studies were then included in this
review. A supplementary approach employed to identify records con­
sisted of hand searching in the reference lists, especially from the pre­
vious reviews on the topic.
A total of 699 records were retrieved and screened for eligibility
(time range of publications 2002–2021). We first excluded studies based
on title and abstract and then reviewed the full text of the remaining 34
articles for potential relevance. Finally, only 11 studies met our inclu­
sion criteria and were therefore included in this review. Please refer to
Fig. 1 for the flowchart depicting the selection process.
From each of the eleven selected studies whose information is sum­
marized in Table 1, the name of authors, year of publication, charac­
teristic of sample/diagnosis, type and modality of intervention, clinical
scales, main results, and secondary outcomes were collected. Concern­
ing the constitution of the samples, most of the studies employed par­
ticipants with mixed ethnicity, with most of them Caucasian, followed
by Asian, Hispanic, and black African/American.

Also, Desnoyers et al. (2016) compared ACT and CBT interventions
in SAD patients (mean age: 34.4 ± 11.1 years). Specifically, they divided
the patients into two 12-week treatment groups, each formed by 53
participants. In this study, the authors considered the self-focused
attention and the tendency for safety behaviors, especially because
they have been found to have a negative impact on social situations in
SAD patients (Hofmann, 2000; Hoffart et al., 2009). However, no sig­
nificant difference between the two treatments was reported, but
significantly lower self-attention (effect sizes d > 0.90) and lower
adoption of safety behaviors (effect sizes d > 1) were found over time in
both groups. Concerning secondary outcomes, safety behaviors medi­
ated the relationship between self-focus attention and social anxiety and
vice versa; self-focus attention was also found to be a mediator in both
ACT and CBT.

Moreover, Sewart et al. (2019) used positive and negative effects as
potential outcomes and moderators of CBT and ACT and compared the
trajectories of these variables in two groups of SAD patients after a 12weekly individual therapy (CBT n = 45, ACT n = 35; overall mean
age: 28.3 ± 6.7 years), with a waiting list control group (N = 31). Of
interest, the authors observed a reduction of patients' negative affect
(including fear and anxiety) and an increase of positive affect in both
CBT and ACT. However, ACT was more effective in reducing negative
affect, a result that was not seen in the CBT group.
In this clinical trial carried out by Mesri et al. (2017), 49 individuals,
divided into two groups, received a 12 weekly individual CBT (n = 28,
mean age: 28.18 ± 6.54 years) or ACT (n = 24, mean age: 28.78 ± 6.05
years) psychotherapy. The authors demonstrated that public speaking
avoidance was found to be a solid moderator of outcome measures,
which was also observed during the 12-month follow-up, ultimately
suggesting that the more behaviourally avoidant individuals during a

social avoidance was not found to be a significant moderator of any
outcome measure. Similarly, Barrera et al. (2016) conducted an inter­
esting brief experiment considering public speaking in 41 SAD patients
(mean age: 29 ± 5.5 years). All subjects that reported fear of public
speaking were asked to perform the same exposure task (Esp.), a typical
behavioral technique. After exposure (public speaking performance) all
subjects were randomized into 3 groups: Esp. only, Esp. + ACT and Esp.
+ CBT. Specifically, the ACT group underwent the cognitive defusion
process (a typical ACT intervention) whereas the CBT group was
exposed to the cognitive restructuring process (a typical CBT interven­
tion). From this experiment, it emerged that in a very short period, the
patients exposed to either the ACT or CBT conditions had similar de­
creases in discomfort related to negative thoughts (effect sizes d > 0.5).
As secondary outcomes, the authors found a decrease in perceived ac­
curacy of negative thoughts in all three conditions and a decrease in the
perceived importance of negative thoughts only in the Esp. + ACT
group. The fear of “public speaking” was also evaluated in a controlled
trial by Block and Wulfert (2000), in which they tested the relative ef­
ficacy of ACT as compared to Cognitive-Behavioral Group Therapy
(CBGT). Specifically, 11 students with SAD were assigned to ACT
treatment (n = 3) or CBGT (n = 4) condition, each consisting of four 1 1/
2 h sessions held at weekly intervals. The remaining participants
belonged to the wait-list control condition (n = 4). Both participants in
the ACT and CBGT conditions reported clinical improvement on social
anxiety, while ACT seemed to slightly favor an increase in willingness to
engage in feared situations, especially at the three-month follow-up
assessment.
Furthermore, three studies aimed to investigate the effectiveness of
the ACT in SAD, by comparing an experimental group that received the
treatment, with a waiting list group receiving no treatment. In all these
studies, a significant difference emerged in the scores of the scales
administered, highlighting the effectiveness of the ACT in reducing the
symptoms of social anxiety (Yadegari et al., 2014; Khoramnia et al.,
2020), external shame (Khoramnia et al., 2020) and increasing psy­
chological flexibility (Azadeh et al., 2016; Khoramnia et al., 2020).
In more details, the study by Khoramnia et al. (2020) conducted on
24 students with SAD (mean age: 22.12 ± 1.08 years), analyzed the
treatment completers of twelve 90-min ACT session protocols developed
by Eifert et al. (2009). The psychotherapy included psychoeducation
and focused on acceptance and commitment to pursue a value-based life
by creating new behavioral patterns. Following the post-test and the two
months follow-up stages, the experimental group (n = 11, mean age:
23.11 ± 1.01 years) reported reduced a) external shame (effect size pre
vs post test d = 0.33; effect size pre vs follow-up d = 0.86), b) social
anxiety (effect size pre vs post test d = 0.31; effect size pre vs follow-up d
= 0.7), c) difficulty in emotional regulation (effect size pre vs post test d
= 0.87; effect size pre vs follow-up d = 0.88), and d) lack of acceptance
of emotional responses (effect size pre vs post test d = − 1.73; effect size
pre vs follow-up d = − 0.25), compared to the control group (n = 11,
mean age: 21.13 ± 1.09 years). Also, the effectiveness of ACT was shown
by the presence of an increase in self-compassion (effect size pre vs post
test d = − 1.66; effect size pre vs follow-up d = − 1.24) and a 43% in­
crease in psychological flexibility, which in the follow-up stage, showed
a further increase of 67% in the experimental group.
Azadeh et al. (2016) showed that in the post-test stage, the ACT
reduced interpersonal problems (effect size d = 1.55) and increased
psychological flexibility (effect size d = 1.19) in the experimental group
consisting of 15 SAD female high school students, which were compared
to 15 controls (overall mean age: 15.43 ± 0.78 years). Specifically, after
the ten 90-min weekly sessions, the authors found a significant differ­
ence in psychological flexibility between controls and SAD patients,
which in turn had increased behavioral repertoire when facing stressful
and annoying situations.
Yadegari et al. (2014) randomly assigned a sample of 16 young
adults suffering from SAD to an ACT treatment protocol of 12-sessions

(n = 8, mean age: 22.38 ± 1.55 years) and to a wait-list group that
did not receive any treatment (n = 8, mean age: 23.5 ± 1.96 years). The
ACT protocol was developed based on the acceptance and commitment
group therapy for SAD (Fleming and Kocovski, 2009). The protocol
consisted (among the main goals) in introducing the idea of defusion
with social anxiety and the feelings resulting from it, highlighting the
importance of personal values as a guide for actions. The authors found
that 12 sessions of ACT were effective in significantly reducing symp­
toms of social anxiety among the participants in the experimental group
(effect size d = 2.36), although compared to the control group there was
not much difference between the pre-test and post-test scores.
Finally, the study by Clarke et al. (2020) explored the effect of only
ACT interventions in 6 SAD participants (mean age: 20.33 ± 1.37 years),
without any control group. The authors found greater psychological
flexibility (effect size pre vs post d = − 1.3) and decreased performance
anxiety symptoms effect size pre vs post d = 1.11) in six vocal students
with music performance anxiety, which may be considered a subtype of
SAD, treated with six consecutive weeks of individual ACT group-based
sessions. Furthermore, the progress was maintained after the 3-month
follow-up (effect size pre vs follow-up d = − 1.66 and 1.21). Within
the secondary outcomes, the authors found that in the post-test stage,
SAD patients showed a decrease in levels of depression, generalized
anxiety, and stress while the improvement in wellbeing was not main­
tained at the follow-up.
4. Discussion
Although further investigations exploring the psychological factors
and mechanisms of change that occur during this treatment are still
needed, overall, the results of the reviewed studies suggest that ACT may
be considered a promising treatment for reducing the symptoms of SAD.
Indeed, the reviewed studies that considered only the ACT inter­
vention for the treatment of social phobia reported its effectiveness for
developing psychological flexibility, defusion, connection, and “accep­
tance” of the anxiety symptoms that may be considered as part of the
SAD's psychological functioning.
These results are particularly noteworthy since, as postulated by ACT
theory, the acceptance of disturbing experiences, including feelings and
their connected thoughts, cognitive defusion, cognitive detachment for
specific thinking, and living in the moment, may play a key role in
increasing subjective well-being (Hayes et al., 1999). Also, the treatment
process including the specification of values and commitment to them
may ultimately improve the quality of life and psychological flexibility
in social anxiety.
Additionally, from the results it emerged that the ACT treatment
effectively reduced the feelings of shame that affect experiential
avoidance (Etzel, 2006), which is one of the criteria of psychological
inflexibility in the ACT, by reducing fear and concern about public sit­
uations and negative judgments. Interestingly, the improvement was
also observed in self-compassion, which, although it is not a target
variable of the ACT, could be a powerful mediator of the effectiveness of
this treatment (Vowles et al., 2014).
Overall, these results point towards the hypothesis that ACT, similar
to the traditional CBT, leads to a decrease in discomfort related to so­
cially anxious thoughts. This is particularly achieved by improving selfattention, awareness, and safety behaviors by guiding the patient to
open up to the unpleasant experiences without trying to control them
unreasonably and through mindfulness or acceptance techniques used to
avoid excessive control. These results are not surprising since, although
the primary goal of ACT is not to regulate emotions but to accept the
life's painful sides that inevitably come with it, some studies reported
that emotion regulation is a result of ACT (Arch and Craske, 2008), as
also confirmed by Niles et al. (2013) and Khoramnia et al. (2020).
Moreover, the implementation of emotion regulation strategies learned
during traditional cognitive psychotherapy could be strictly connected
to the development of better well-being and socioeconomic

connection with it, aspects that can be only explored in a longer-term
perspective. Third, the lack of a control group limited the ability to
investigate the processes of change and to verify the effectiveness of
treatment, while the administration of group- or individual-based ACT
therapies also limited the comparison of the results. Fourth, the meth­
odological approach differs across the available studies, especially in
terms of the psychological variables considered (often self-assessed and
therefore influenced by social desirability). Given that, SAD is a het­
erogeneous diagnostic category and thereforeall main cognitive factors
implicated should be considered as they may lead to maintenance and
further exacerbation of the social phobia (Hofmann, 2007) as well as to
the disruption of the psychological process of change. Fifth, none of the
reviewed studies considered the importance of the therapeutic rela­
tionship (Mulder et al., 2017), a factor that could be responsible for the
variability of patients' outcomes after specific treatments. Finally,
further relevant limitations were associated with the presence of dif­
ferences in the sample sizes, often very small or composed of young
females, and the variability in the duration and numbers of the psy­
chotherapy sessions. All these aspects could have limited the general­
izability of the results. In addition, since the reviewed studies did not
stratify the results according to the different ethnicity, it was not
possible to explore their impact in the treatment of ACT on SAD.

achievement, as previously demonstrated by Côté et al. (2010). Indeed,
since SAD individuals are perceived to have little control over their
anxiety, the regulation of their emotions is a very important part of the
psychopathological cycle that maintains the disorder (Hofmann, 2007).
Furthermore, from the results of some of the reviewed studies, it
appears that the negative affect seems to decrease significantly after
both ACT and CBT treatments. In literature, the negative affect has been
linked to a reaction of the human defense system, which generates fear
and anxiety (Davidson, 1994) and serves to avoidance of perceived
threats and aversive outcomes (Gray, 1994). Therefore, these results are
not surprising especially because the traditional CBT for anxiety disor­
ders has been designed to specifically target the negative affect associ­
ated with defense mechanisms, with a study also showing a better
outcome after ACT (Sewart et al., 2019). Also, in this case, this result is
not surprising especially because ACT, which is mainly based on
mindfulness skills (including accepting events without evaluation), has
been found to improve emotional reactivity, and cause a subsequent
change in social anxiety (Kocovski et al., 2015), through the use of the
observational function (Gu et al., 2015; Scher et al., 2005). However,
although the precepts of mindfulness are not explicitly discussed in
traditional cognitive psychotherapy, it appears that this shift in aware­
ness also occurs after CBT treatment (Kocovski et al., 2015).
Notably, overall these observations suggest that ACT and CBT ap­
proaches can be effective in treating social phobia, probably because
they share common psychological mechanisms, which need to be further
explored in future studies. This finding is not surprising especially
because the two cognitive treatments can be considered complementary,
although they focus on different goals (cognitive restructuring versus
acceptance).
In particular, ACT could be used to increase attention to mental
acceptance and flexibility, which in turn leads to improved selfperception of symptoms. Instead, traditional CBT has the task of pro­
moting behavioral exposure and of inducing cognitive processes during
the interaction with the therapist. Finally, consistent with the concep­
tual foundations and strategies of both treatments, Block and Wulfert
(2000) found a slight difference that favored CBT for anxiety reduction,
through changing of beliefs, and the ACT for increased willingness to
engage in feared situations, regardless of changes in anxiety. Therefore,
these findings suggest that although these treatments are complemen­
tary, they also demonstrate some differences in terms of outcome and
processes used in SAD.

5. Conclusions
From the above-mentioned studies, it emerged that ACT could be
considered a promising treatment for social phobia (Twohig et al., 2006;
Pankowski et al., 2017; O’Donoghue et al., 2018). However, larger and
more homogeneous studies are needed to confirm the efficacy of this
treatment in this complex psychiatric disorder.

4.1. Limitations

Conflict of interest

Although a comprehensive overview of the literature has been per­
formed, this review suffers from some limitations. Specifically, we only
considered original articles that used the English language, which can be
considered a major limitation. Also, we did not measure the internal
validity of individual eligible trials, therefore we were not able to rule
out the risk of publication bias and the risk of bias between studies
generated by their heterogeneity.
Furthermore, despite the above-mentioned results, the reviewed
studies are also affected by some limitations that could affect the
interpretation of their findings.
First, all included except one (Sewart et al., 2019), used a treatment
completers approach, analyzing only participants who completed the
study despite the bias associated with this choice. Sewart et al. (2019) by
contrast, provided a more accurate estimate of treatment efficacy by
carrying out an intent-to-treat analysis, also including participants who
dropped out of the study. Second, concerning the study design, only one
of the reviewed studies considered an appropriate follow-up time,
especially because the study by Mesri et al. (2017) highlighted that the
results of ACT or CBT therapy may be more evident after a 12-month
follow-up. This is an important limitation because a longitudinal

Long-term outcomes of cognitive behavioural therapy for social anxiety
disorder: A meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
Reuben Kindred, Glen W. Bates *, Nicholas L. McBride
Department of Psychological Sciences, Swinburne University of Technology, John St, Hawthorn 3122, Australia

ARTICLEINFO

ABSTRACT

Keywords:
Social anxiety disorder
Cognitive behavioural therapy
Randomized controlled trials
Long-term outcomes
Meta-analysis

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is effective in treating Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD). However, less is
known about whether gains achieved in disorder-specific and secondary outcomes (e.g., depression, general
anxiety, quality of life, and self-esteem) are maintained 12 months or longer. A systematic literature search
yielded 25 relevant studies that administered CBT to participants with SAD. Multivariate meta-analyses of posttreatment assessments, found that CBT was superior to control conditions in reducing social anxiety (g =.74),
depression (g =.52), general anxiety (g =.69) and improving quality of life (g =.39). The within-groups effect
sizes revealed that 12 months or more after CBT treatment, symptoms continued to improve for social anxiety
(gav =.23) and quality of life (gav =.17), and gains were maintained for depressive (gav =.06) and general anxiety
symptoms (gav =.03). However, meta-analyses of long-term outcomes lack comparison groups. Moderation was
non-significant for the treatment model, format, number of sessions, treatment duration, or inclusion of booster
sessions. Future research may investigate what drives improvement after treatment cessation and how CBT af­
fects other co-occurring symptomatology. Taken together, CBT produces many benefits for SAD and individuals
with co-occurring symptoms can benefit from extant SAD-focused treatments.

1. Introduction

1.1. Long-term efficacy of cognitive behavioural therapy

Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) is an anxiety disorder marked by
extreme fear of negative evaluation in social situations (American Psy­
chiatric Association, 2022). SAD causes considerable distress and
impaired ability to function in daily life (Heeren et al., 2017), for
example, difficulty engaging in social encounters, school dropout, and
employment disruption are common. It is one of the most frequently
diagnosed disorders, with lifetime prevalence rates of 8.4 % in Austra­
lian adults (Crome et al., 2015) and 13.0 % in American adults (Kessler
et al., 2012). High rates of comorbidity (Stuhldreher et al., 2014) and
co-occurrence are common with depression (Farmer et al., 2014;
Koyuncu et al., 2015), generalised anxiety (Koyuncu et al., 2019), low
quality of life (Dryman et al., 2016), and low self-esteem (Iancu et al.,
2015). Given that SAD follows a chronic and debilitating course if un­
treated (Blanco et al., 2011; Steinert et al., 2013), it is crucial to identify
treatments that can target a broad array of symptomatology and remain
efficacious long term.

Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is considered the ‘gold-stan­
dard’ treatment for SAD (David et al., 2018; Levy et al., 2021) and
previous meta-analyses have established its efficacy at posttreatment
assessment (Mayo-Wilson et al., 2014; Powers et al., 2008). However,
few meta-analyses have examined the long-term outcome studies that
are available (Pelissolo et al., 2019). To clarify the true effects of
treatment, it is important to explicate long-term outcomes, as solely
assessing outcomes at posttreatment may underestimate effect sizes if
treatments produce lags in symptom reduction. The current
meta-analysis operationalizes long term as 12 months after treatment
cessation. At 12 months or longer post treatment, there is little variance
in gains (Anderson et al., 2017; Mortberg et al., 2007), indicating that
gains have stabilised by this time.
There have been four previous meta-analyses of long-term outcomes
of SAD treatment. However, these studies are severely limited in
methodological quality. The most recent study by Van Dis et al. (2020)

3) for CBT treatments from pre-treatment to 12-month or longer
follow-up. However, none of the three studies were of high quality — as
they were considered high risk in at least one criterion for the study
design quality measure — and the study with the largest weight (i.e.,
Furmark et al., 2009) was incorrectly classified as having a long-term
waitlist, meaning the outcome of the intervention group at follow-up
was compared to the control group’s outcome at post-treatment,
obfuscating the summary effect size. Moreover, such pre-treatment to
follow-up summary estimates do not delineate the effect of active and
inactive treatment. Another meta-analysis, Acarturk et al. (2009), found
a small (d = 0.15, 95 % CI: 0.01—0.29) effect size from post-treatment
assessment to ≥ 7-month follow-up in nine studies. No restrictions were
applied psychological treatment, this resulted in high clinical hetero­
geneity. In these cases, when interacting factors of treatment variables
(e.g., treatment length or format) are not accounted for, the contribution
towards clinical decision-making is limited (Kriston, 2013), as such ef­
fect estimates often obscure differences in treatment characteristics that
are clinically meaningful (Wang et al., 2007). Additionally, instead of an
Intention-To-Treat (ITT) analysis that is crucial in reliably estimating the
effect size (McCoy, 2017), most of the included studies used a
Completers-Only (CO) analysis. Prior to this, two further meta-analyses
measured effect sizes with follow-up data (Gould et al., 1997; Taylor,
1996) from studies that were not Randomised Controlled Trials (RCTs).
RCTs minimise selection bias with random assignment and provide the
most reliable estimate of treatment by comparisons made to a control
group. However, employment of a control group when assessing
long-term outcomes is considered unethical — as it disallows partici­
pants to seek treatment — and trials with such designs are often
outdated, non-randomised, or have a high risk of bias. As such, RCTs
assessing long-term outcomes of treatment are often limited to
within-groups study designs, which may partly explain the paucity of
reviews that consider the long-term outcomes of SAD treatment, or be an
important limitation of such reviews, including the current paper.
Broad categories of subsyndromal symptoms, and their chronicity,
have also gone under-reported in meta-analytic examinations of SAD
treatment. For all SAD psychological treatments, Acarturk et al. (2009)
found a large effect size of d = 0.70 (95 % CI: 0.46—0.94, k = 19) for
depression and d = 0.70 (95 % CI: 0.47—0.93, k = 16) for general
anxiety — however, whether such treatment gains were maintained or
fluctuated long-term was not analysed. Regarding quality of life,
Kampmann et al. (2016) focused on Internet-based CBT (i-CBT) studies
and found a large effect size of g = 0.63 (95 % CI: 0.06—1.20, k = 2) at
six months after treatment cessation, but whether a lag effect was
apparent is uncertain. In general, there is a dearth of research on the
chronicity of secondary outcomes in the treatment of SAD, making it
difficult to assess the comprehensiveness of treatment results. However,
more recent trials have assessed a broader scope of symptomatology,
and included long-term follow-ups, allowing for an examination of
long-term outcomes in this paper.

(2014), the Clark and Wells model outperformed the Heimberg model,
with non-overlapping confidence intervals. However, implementation of
a network meta-analysis, which suffer from inherent error inflation
problems, and inaccuracies in how treatments were coded were identi­
fied as shortcomings of this paper (Wampold et al., 2017). Compared to
face-to-face treatments, meta-analyses reveal i-CBT reaches equivalent
(Andersson et al., 2014) or slightly more modest effect sizes (Mayo-­
Wilson et al., 2014).
The contribution of specific treatment characteristics has yet to be
examined in meta-analyses. Whilst the number of treatment sessions
does not appear to impact treatment efficacy (Powers et al., 2008),
research has not considered the effect of treatment duration, total
treatment hours, and booster sessions. Determining whether these
methodological characteristics are influential may shape recommenda­
tions for clinicians.
1.3. The present study
The current meta-analysis had three aims. First, to evaluate the ef­
ficacy of CBTRCTs on the long-term disorder-specific outcomes of SAD.
Second, to examine the effects of CBT for SAD on long-term, sub­
syndromal secondary outcomes, including depression, general anxiety,
quality of life, and self-esteem. Assuming statistical heterogeneity was
present, the third aim was to assess the influence of potential moderators
of treatment efficacy including: treatment model, format, treatment
duration, number of prescribed treatment sessions, and inclusion of
booster sessions.
2. Method
2.1. Protocol and registration
This meta-analysis followed the guidelines of Preferred Reporting
Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA/PRISMA-S).
The protocol was registered with PROSPEROID: CRD42021244768.
2.2. Identification and selection of studies
A literature search was conducted on the 13th of December, 2020
and then rerun on the 1st of September, 2021, and the 1st of January,
2022. Eight electronic databases were searched: Web of Science Core
Collection, PsycINFO, PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of
Controlled Trials, and the Cumulative Index of Nursing and Allied
Health Literature (CINAHL). To find unpublished studies, the ProQuest
Dissertations and Theses and ProQuest Central databases were searched.
Search terms were “social anxiety” OR “social phobia” OR “social
phobic” OR “speaking fear.” To increase the search sensitivity, we did
not limit the results by searching for terms indicative of RCTs. No lan­
guage restrictions were applied. A translator was enlisted to translate an
included study published in Spanish (Antón & Olivares-Olivares, 2012).
Details of the search strategy are supplied in Appendix A. Records were
first imported into Endnote X9 and duplicates removed with the dupli­
cate identification strategy. Titles and abstracts were screened by RK
and papers that were at risk of false exclusion were reviewed with
co-authors. Full texts were then obtained.
Studies were included if they (1) examined the effects of a CBT-based
intervention for SAD, Generalized Social Anxiety Disorder (GSAD), or
Fear of Public Speaking (FOPS), in (2) had participants aged 18 years or
older (3) with a clinical diagnosis of SAD, (4) were compared with a
control group (5) in an RCT. Studies required (6) a calculable stan­
dardized mean difference (SMD) and (7) a ≥ 12-month follow-up
assessment. As all relevant papers had a calculable SMD, no authors
were needed to be contacted for this information. Studies were excluded
if they contained less than 10 cases at randomisation to mitigate against
small-study effects that may distort summary effect sizes (Turner et al.,

1.2. Potential moderators of outcome
CBT is not a unitary intervention protocol and there are various
potential moderators of outcome that may be clinically important. For
SAD, two frequently cited CBT treatment models are the Heimberg
model (Rapee & Heimberg, 1997), often administered in a group format,
but has been efficacious when administered individually (Goldin et al.,
2012; Ledley et al., 2009); and the Clark and Wells model (1995), pri­
marily administered in an individual format, but has also been adapted
to the group setting (Mortberg et al., 2007; Stangier et al., 2003). The
i-CBT format, a type of self-guided therapy, is also becoming increas­
ingly common.
There is mixed evidence of statistical heterogeneity within CBT
models and formats. Powers et al. (2008) found no statistically signifi­
cant difference between CBT interventions. Acarturk et al. (2009) found

The RoB 2.0 Cochrane Handbook Risk of Bias Assessment Tool
version 6.1 (Higgins & Thomas, 2020) was used to establish an overall
risk-of-bias judgement based on five domains: randomisation process,
deviations from intended interventions, missing outcome data, mea­
surement of the outcome, and selection of the reported result. For the
missing outcome data domain, data were considered available for
almost all participants if the dropout rate was both ≤ 5% at posttreatment and ≤ 20 % at 12-month or next longest follow-up — as per
suggestions that rates higher than these are a threat to study validity
(Dettori, 2011; Fewtrell et al., 2008). Assessment of bias and treatment
quality assessment was conducted by RK and NM independently, with
discrepancies being resolved by discussion.

2.3. Coding procedure and data extraction
The included studies were coded on variables regarding study
characteristics and specific characteristics such as treatment model,
treatment format, control group type, treatment hours and duration,
number of sessions, the inclusion of booster sessions, type of data
analysis, and duration of follow-up. Data extraction was conducted by
RK and NM, with discrepancies resolved by discussion.

2.5. Data analysis plan
2.5.1. Quantitative synthesis
Pairwise meta-analyses were conducted to obtain an effect estimate
of CBT interventions relative to a control group. This methodology was
chosen over a network meta-analysis, which may result in inflated error
rates (Efthimiou & White, 2020) that have likely contributed to repli­
cation failures of meta-analytic examinations of SAD treatment (Wam­
pold et al., 2017), often lack power to detect inconsistency between
direct and indirect comparisons (Veroniki et al., 2014), and are
preferred when the research focus is broad in scope (Rouse et al., 2017).

2.4. Treatment quality and risk of bias assessment
Treatment quality was assessed by three criteria for evaluating
empirically supported psychological interventions (Chambless & Hol­
lon, 1998). Criteria were as follows: (1) the study employed a treatment
manual, (2) therapists were trained for the specific intervention, and (3)
treatment integrity was present by way of therapist supervision, reviews
of treatment session recordings, or adherence to a measurement

2.5.2. Measures
Effect sizes were calculated for social anxiety, depression, general
anxiety and quality of life outcomes. Only validated measures were used

(see Appendix B). Whilst self-esteem measures and clinician-rated
measures for social anxiety were planned to be synthesised, few
studies included these (k ≤ 3), therefore, these were not meta-analysed.
Where studies included multiple measures for the same outcome, as was
often the case with social anxiety symptoms, these measures were
aggregated within studies to create a single combined effect for each
study.

2.5.5. Heterogeneity and moderator analyses
Cochran’s Q chi-squared test was calculated to test significance in the
variation of study results that were not due to chance. A statistically
significant Q rejects the null hypothesis of homogeneity. To quantify the
percentage of variance remaining if sampling error could be removed,
the Higgins I2 statistic was calculated along with its 95 % CI. A common
interpretation for I2 is that 25 % equates to low, 50 % to moderate, and
75 % to high heterogeneity (Borenstein et al., 2009). If heterogeneity
reached significance at p < .05 of Cochran’s Q statistic, a
meta-regression analysis was conducted. To test robustness of the
meta-regression, permutation tests with 10,000 iterations were con­
ducted for moderators that were p < .20 (Higgins & Thompson, 2004).
Meta-regressions were only considered if k ≥ 5, the required number of
studies for permutation tests to be able to obtain a p-value less than.05
(Viechtbauer et al., 2015).

2.5.3. Calculation of effect sizes
When calculating effect sizes, ITT data were preferred over CO data.
If a study did not report means and standard deviations, alternative
statistics (e.g., t-value, p-value) were used. The authors were contacted if
trials contained incomplete data (k = 2, response rate = 50 %). As such,
unpublished data from one study (Goldin et al., 2016) were included,
and the data from depression measures in one study (Botella et al., 2010)
were excluded.
Calculations of weighted mean effect sizes, statistical heterogeneity,
and moderator analyses were conducted with the metafor package
version 3.0–2 (Viechtbauer, 2010) in version 4.0.3 of R (RCore Team,
2018). The random effects model was chosen to calculate the mean ef­
fect size for each meta-analysis. This model takes into account the true
variation in effect size due to systematic differences between studies,
resulting in robust estimations of the mean effect size (Hedges & Vevea,
1998).

2.5.6. Publication bias
The symmetry of the funnel plot was tested with Egger’s test of the
intercept (Egger et al., 1997). Additionally, a trim-and-fill procedure
(Duval & Tweedie, 2000) was run to create an adjusted effect size by
controlling for publication bias.
3. Results
3.1. Selection and characteristics of studies

2.5.3.1. Controlled between-groups effect size. To measure the efficacy of
the intervention, a controlled, between-groups effect size was calcu­
lated, which compares the treatment group to the control group at posttreatment. The Hedge’s g effect size was calculated by finding the mean
difference between the treatment and control group at post-treatment
and dividing this figure by the pooled weighted standard deviation
(Hedges & Olkin, 1985). Following this, a small sample bias correction
(Lipsey & Wilson, 2001) was applied: J = 1 − (3/(4df− 1)). As Hedge’s g
belongs to the SMD effect size family, effect sizes are commonly inter­
preted as small (d/g = 0.2), medium (d/g = 0.5), and large (d/g = 0.8)
based on benchmarks suggested by Cohen (1988), although these should
be considered as arbitrary (Thompson, 2007).

The systematic search yielded a total of 25 RCTs that met all the
inclusion criteria. In total, 1902 participants were included in this metaanalysis from the treatment groups. Studies included follow-up assess­
ments either at 12 months (k = 23), 15 months (k = 1) or 18 months
(k = 1). Models of face-to-face treatments were that of Clark & Wells
(k = 9), Heimberg (k = 5), or otherwise general or unspecified CBT
(k = 5). There were six i-CBT studies. Treatments were administered
individually (k = 18) or in a group (k = 7). Measurable outcomes were
available for self-rated social anxiety (k = 25), depressive symptoms
(k = 13), general anxiety (k = 9), and quality of life (k = 5). Fourteen of
the included trials either reported overall or specific comorbidities of
participants — this amounted to 57.16 % of treatment participants
captured in the current meta-analysis as having their comorbidity re­
ported within a RCT. Of RCTs that reported comorbidities, the pointprevalence of comorbidity was 45.73 % of participants, however, this
is likely an underestimate, as RCTs often screened for either only Axis I
or Axis II disorders. Table 1 presents the study characteristics.

2.5.3.2. Uncontrolled within-groups effect size. Long-term effects of CBT
on SAD were assessed by calculating the uncontrolled within-groups
effect size, which measures the change in symptoms for the treatment
group from post-treatment to long-term follow-up. Hedges gav was
employed as this most closely resembles between-groups Hedges g
(Caldwell & Vigotsky, 2020), however, whilst the current index provides
an estimation of the effect size more similar to those with intergroup
designs, it may be affected by maturation, history, or testing effects
(Rubio-Aparicio et al., 2018). As values for the treatment group at
post-treatment and follow-up are not independent of each other, a
conservative correlation of r = 0.70 between these scores was assumed
to calculate Hedges gav. Unlike the between-groups effect size, any
within-groups effect size was considered meaningful. For instance, gav
= 0 indicates that treatment gains have been maintained long-term.
However, if the 95 % CI of gav does not overlap with 0, it indicates a
statistically significant change (i.e., improvement or decline after
treatment).

3.2. Treatment quality
Several studies did not sufficiently examine whether treatment was
implemented as intended. For face-to-face treatments (k = 19), the
treatment quality score was 2.37/3. A treatment manual was utilized in
13 studies, whilst 16 studies trained therapists for the specific treatment,
and 16 studies checked for treatment integrity.
3.3. Risk of bias
The risk of bias varied across studies (see Appendix C). Bias may arise
in the randomisation process due to a lack of information regarding
concealment of allocation sequence or baseline differences. Within this
domain, bias was high in one study, and there were some concerns in
five studies. Deviations from intended interventions was a high risk of
bias in five studies due to use of a CO analysis. Bias arising from missing
outcome data was deemed high for nine studies, most often due to
failure to explain how missing data was handled. As masking of pro­
viders is impossible in psychological interventions, no trials were
considered at risk in this domain. Most trials were not registered or
comprehensively reported leading to some concerns for 22 studies in the
selection of the reported result domain. This was not unexpected, as

2.5.4. Random variance estimation
To derive τ2, the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator
was utilised, as it has a low bias (Langan et al., 2019) and is recom­
mended for continuous outcome meta-analyses (Novianti et al., 2014).
The Knapp and Hartung (2003) adjustment was also applied, as it factors
in residual heterogeneity uncertainty by adjusting the standard errors of
the estimate’s coefficients, resulting in conservative confidence intervals
(IntHout et al., 2014).
