(CBT) to be effective in treating social anxiety disorder (SAD). Yet, less is known
routine clinical practice. In this study, 231 patients with SAD were treated with CBT
under routine conditions and were examined at pre- and post-treatment as well as at
6 and 12 months follow-up. We applied self-reports to assess symptoms of SAD
(defined as primary outcome), depression and psychological distress (defined as secondary outcome). We conducted both completer and intent-to-treat analyses and
also assessed the reliability of change with the reliable change index. Results revealed
significant reductions in symptoms of SAD between pre- and post-assessments, with
effect sizes ranging from d = 0.9 to 1.2. Depending on the SAD specific questionnaire applied, 47.8% to 73.5% of the sample showed a reliable positive change,
whereas 1.9% to 3.8% showed a reliable negative change. Depressive symptoms and
psychological distress also decreased significantly from pre- to post-assessment, with
large effect sizes. Significant treatment gains regarding both primary and secondary
outcomes were further observed at 6 and 12 months follow-up. The current findings
based on a large sample of patients suggest that psychotherapists in CBT training
working under routine conditions can effectively treat symptoms of SAD, depression
and psychological distress.

Another limitation is that we did not control for the effects of unspecific treatment factors (e.g. therapeutic alliance). Finally, no clinicianadministered measures were conducted by independent clinical raters.
In conclusion, our findings provide evidence that CBT can effectively reduce SAD and comorbid symptoms in naturalistic settings.
The findings further demonstrate that therapists in training can effectively treat patients with SAD. The validity of the current findings is
supported by calculating and reporting reliability of change scores as
well as by assessing treatment gains up to 1 year after treatment.
Future research needs to investigate which therapeutic elements are
mostly associated with behaviour change as well as the needed
amount of sessions to achieve a reliable change of SAD and related

Effectiveness of virtual reality and in vivo exposure combined
with Acceptance and Commitment Therapy for public speaking
anxiety: a randomized clinical trial
Francisco Montesinos1
David Lobato1

· Christian Calderón-Pozo1

· Juan M. Flujas-Contreras2

· Sonia Diéguez3

·

Accepted: 27 July 2025
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025

Abstract
Fear of public speaking (PSF) is one of the primary manifestations of social phobia and is highly prevalent among university students. In vivo (IV) exposure from Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) has proven effective for treating PSF. Exposure through virtual reality (VR) offers practical advantages over IV exposure, although its effectiveness
still needs to be demonstrated. This study aims to provide evidence for ACT-based VR in treating PSF. This randomized
clinical trial involved thirty-seven university students with significant levels of social phobia and PSF. Participants were
randomly assigned to ACT-based IV exposure, ACT-based VR, or a waiting list. Those on the waiting list were later
allocated to either IV or ACT conditions. A five-session ACT-based individual treatment protocol was administered. Measures were collected using standardized questionnaires and subjective scales before and after treatment, as well as at a
three-month follow-up. Both IV and VRACT-based interventions were found to be feasible in a university setting, with
most participants showing excellent adherence. Results demonstrated the interventions’ impact on PSF, social anxiety,
cognitive fusion, and self-efficacy levels, with moderate to large effect sizes. ACT-based interventions were more successful in reducing PSF compared to non-intervention. Exposure aimed at psychological acceptance proved effective, and
the practical advantages of VR were confirmed. This study provides evidence for delivering ACT-based exposure through
VR for treating PSF in a university context. Future research should aim to provide additional evidence with broader and
more diverse samples.
Keywords Acceptance and Commitment Therapy · Anxiety disorders · In vivo exposure · Psychological flexibility ·
Public speaking fear · Virtual reality

Introduction
Oral presentation is a core competency among higher education students. European policymakers have emphasized the
need to incorporate oral presentation skills into university
qualifications (The Council of the European Union, 2018).
Public speaking competence is essential in both academic and
professional settings, and universities should therefore prepare students to excel in this area (Becerra, 2017). However,
research indicates that graduates often begin their professional
careers with inadequate oral presentation skills (Gray, 2010),
and feel that their education has not sufficiently developed
these skills (Observatorio de Innovación en el Empleo, 2017).
Public speaking difficulties typically arise in the context
of oral presentations. This situation is considered stressful

for many individuals, triggering catastrophic anticipations
(Orejudo et al., 2007) and psychophysiological responses
indicative of anxiety, such as increased sweating, heart rate,
and gastric symptoms (Bodie, 2010). The frequency and
intensity of this fear are influenced by environmental and
contextual variables, such as speaking in unfamiliar settings,
addressing large audiences, differences in status between
the speaker and the audience, or having limited knowledge
of the topic (Orejudo et al., 2007). To alleviate the discomfort these situations generate, they are often avoided, resulting in limited opportunities to learn to function effectively.
While this avoidance may provide temporary relief from
anxiety, it reinforces negative expectations and increases the
likelihood of future avoidance (Bados, 2009).
Public speaking fear (PSF) is a central manifestation of
social phobia according to the DSM-5 (APA, 2013) and
ICD-11 (World Health Organization, 2022). PSF is the most
common social fear not only among individuals with social
phobia but also in the general population (Ruscio et al.,
2008). Scientific literature reports that students exhibit high
levels of PSF, affecting 61% of students in the US (Dwyer
& Davidson, 2012), 64% in Brazil (Ferreira Marinho et al.,
2015), and 51% in Spain (Observatorio de Innovación en el
Empleo, 2017). Given the high prevalence of public speaking
fear, it is crucial to understand the available interventions and
their effectiveness in addressing this common anxiety. Cognitive behavioral therapies (CBT) based on in vivo (IV) exposure are considered the most effective against PSF (Smits &
Hofmann, 2008). IV exposure involves individuals systematically progressing through a hierarchy of scenarios ranked
according to the level of fear they evoke (Reeves et al., 2022).
In recent years, virtual reality (VR) has also demonstrated its
effectiveness in treating anxiety disorders (Morina, 2015)
and specifically in the cognitive-behavioral treatment of PSF
(Bouchard et al., 2017; Wallach et al., 2009). Among the
advantages of VR are the lower risk of drop-out, greater generalization of learned skills to other contexts, greater control
of the therapist over the exposure, time savings, and practical
benefits by not depending on the collaboration of other people
as required in IV exposure or engaging in exposure training,
especially when the feared stimuli are located outside.
Following Anderson and Molloy (2020) and Botella et
al. (2017), several features of VR technology can enhance
the exposure experience. These features include immersion and presence, which help elicit emotional responses
and facilitate learning through exposure. Personalization
allows the replication of individual situations, creating a
meaningful experience for the patient. Therapist control
and safety enable personalized treatment and management

13

of patient anxiety, supporting the exposure approach. Controlled and graded repetition allows patients to repeatedly
face feared situations in a controlled and safe environment,
which is crucial for progressive desensitization. Additionally, VR provides access to environments that are difficult
to replicate in real life, offering better elicitation of feared
responses than imagination exposure.
Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) (Hayes et
al., 2011) is considered a third-wave CBT (Hayes, 2004)
aimed at promoting psychological flexibility (PF). It focuses
on values and the ability to choose actions aligned with
one’s goals while accepting the discomfort that may accompany these actions. ACT methods do not seek to reduce difficult emotions or thoughts, but rather encourage open and
flexible contact with psychological barriers, allowing room
for discomfort while persevering in meaningful actions that
bring the patient closer to their values (Hayes et al., 2011).
ACT is accumulating evidence for the treatment of PSF,
with studies showing reduced levels of avoidance behavior
and self-reported anxiety, and increases in PF, public speaking confidence, and social skills (Brandrick et al., 2021;
England et al., 2012; Glassman et al., 2016; Kim & Kim,
2012; Spencer et al., 2020).
To date, there have been at least two publications exploring the effectiveness of combining ACT with VR exposure.
Yuen et al. (2019) published two pilot studies applying ACT
in PSF, revealing the feasibility and usefulness of VR. A randomized controlled trial (Gorinelli et al., 2023) compared
VR combined with audio-recorded ACT-based instructions
with waiting list (WL), finding a decline in self-reported
PSF, fear of negative evaluation and a significant increase
in well-being, PF, and self-compassion. Recently, our team
published a pilot ACT-based study with two participants,
showing clinically significant reductions in PSF and social
anxiety after delivering IV exposure or VR (Montesinos
et al., 2023). Given the lack of controlled studies combining ACT and VR, it is necessary to provide more evidence
exploring the therapeutic potential of these combined technologies, which have already shown their usefulness separately in the field of PSF. Additionally, it is important to
explore whether VR can be as effective as IV exposure. If
ACT can be effectively applied to PSF through VR exposure, it could also benefit from the advantages associated
with these new technologies. The objective of this study
is to analyse the effectiveness of exposure in different formats (IV and VR) combined with ACT. The hypotheses to
be tested are that ACT-based intervention is more effective
than no intervention, and that VR is at least as effective as
IV exposure in addressing PSF.

Materials and methods
Design
This study is a randomized clinical trial (parallel assignment) with a partially repeated measure between-group
design, comprising three conditions: (1) ACT-based IV
exposure, (2) ACT-based VR exposure, and (3) control
group (WL). Randomisation was completed using the
“Research Randomizer” website, employing randomly
sized, permeated blocks for each arm (VR and IV) in a 1:1
ratio. Block randomisation was prepared by an investigator with no clinical involvement in the trial. Participants
were assessed at baseline (pre-treatment), at the end of the
program (post-treatment), and three months later (followup). Figure 1 shows CONSORT flow diagram. A total of

95 participants expressed interest in the study and were
assessed (see Fig. 1). Of these, 58 did not meet eligibility
criteria and were excluded. Thirty-seven participants were
randomly allocated to either the VR condition (18 participants) or the IV condition (19 participants). Within the VR
condition, 11 participants were randomly assigned to the
experimental group (immediate intervention), and 7 participants were assigned to the WL. Similarly, within the IV
condition, 11 participants were randomly assigned to the
experimental group and 8 participants in IV condition were
assigned to the WL. 11 participants were randomly assigned
to the experimental group, and 8 participants were assigned
to the WL. Thirty-two participants completed the intervention. Three out of 18 participants in the VR condition and
two out of 19 participants in the IV condition dropped out.
Participants in the WL received treatment five weeks later.

Participants

Social anxiety

Thirty-seven university students aged 18–39 years and
enrolled in Universidad Europea de Madrid participated
in the study between September 2019 and July 2022.
Recruitment was halted during the lockdown period due
to the COVID-19 pandemic. Convenience sampling was
conducted based on participant availability, and no financial incentives were provided for participation. The mean
age was 23.7 (SD = 4.7), and the majority (67.7%) were
women. Most participants were studying health degrees
(19% medicine, 16% nursing, 14% psychology, 11% physical therapy). The majority of participants were Spanish
(70%) and Latin American (24%). They were recruited
at the university through emails, posters and professors.
Inclusion criteria were: (1) student at the Universidad
Europea de Madrid, (2) subjective fear intensity and interference higher than 5/10, and (3) significant social anxiety
measured through LSAS (Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale;
Liebowitz, 1987). Exclusion criteria were: (1) alcohol or
drug abuse, (2) psychotropic drug consumption, (3) undergoing psychological/psychiatric treatment, and (4) serious
mental disorder.

The Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS; Liebowitz, 1987) assesses social anxiety. It is a 24-item, four-point
Likert-type scale. Thirteen items refer to performance anxiety (e.g., eating, drinking), and 11 to social situations (e.g.,
going to a party). Scores range between 0 and 144, with
higher scores in the questionnaire indicating higher levels
of social anxiety and worse outcomes. Scores above 51
indicate significant social anxiety (Zubeidat et al., 2006). It
includes four subscales: fear of social interaction, fear of
performance, avoidance of social interaction, and avoidance
of performance. The Spanish adaptation was validated by
Bobes et al. (1999), showing good internal consistency
(α = 0.88), concurrent and discriminant validities. Our study
also showed good internal consistency (α = 0.88).

Measures
The primary outcome of the study was public speaking fear
(PSF). Secondary outcomes included social anxiety, psychological inflexibility (PI), cognitive fusion, self-efficacy,
self-affirmations, subjective intensity and interference of
fear, and satisfaction with treatment. Most outcomes were
assessed at three points: before the intervention, after the
intervention, and at follow-up. However, subjective intensity and interference of fear were evaluated at the end of
each oral presentation throughout the intervention, and satisfaction with treatment was assessed only at the end of the
intervention. The outcomes were measured using the following questionnaires and subjective scales.

Psychological inflexibility
The Acceptance and Action Questionnaire (AAQ-II; Bond
et al., 2011) is a well-known 7-item, seven-point Likert-type
scale that measures PI. Scores range between 7 and 49, with
higher scores indicating higher levels of PI and worse outcomes. The Spanish version has shown good internal consistency (α = 0.88; Ruiz et al., 2013). In our study, it showed
high internal consistency (α = 0.94).
Cognitive fusion
The Cognitive Fusion Questionnaire (CFQ; Gillanders et
al., 2014) assesses cognitive fusion (the tendency to believe
the literal content of private events). It is a 7-item, sevenpoint Likert-type scale. Scores range between 7 and 49, with
higher scores in the questionnaire indicating higher levels
of cognitive fusion and worse outcomes. It is valid, reliable
and sensitive to the effects of treatment. The Spanish version showed high internal consistency (α = 0.93; Ruiz et al.,
2017), as well as in our own studio (α = 0.902).

Public speaking fear

Self-efficacy

The Personal Report and Confidence as Speaker (PRCS;
Paul, 1966) was used to assess the primary outcome domain
of PSF. We administered the short version by Méndez et al.
(1999) of the Spanish adaptation by Bados (1986). It is a
12-item, five-point Likert-type scale. Scores range between
12 and 60, with higher scores indicating higher levels of
PSF and worse outcomes. The Spanish version has shown
good internal consistency (α = 0.91; Méndez et al., 1999)
and reliability (0.81; Méndez et al., 2004). In our study, the
internal consistency for the short version of the PRCS questionnaire was α = 0.83.

The Public speaking self-efficacy and fear questionnaire
(CAHP-CIHP; Bados, 1986) assesses public speaking selfefficacy and PSF. It is a 12-item, six-point Likert-type scale,
including two subscales (self-efficacy and fear). Scores in
self-efficacy subscale range between 12 and 72, with higher
scores in the self-efficacy subscale indicating higher levels of public speaking self-efficacy and better outcomes.
Scores in PSF subscale range between 12 and 72, with
higher scores in the fear subscale indicating higher levels
of PSF and worse outcomes. A previous study by or team
(Montesinos et al., 2025) (n = 575 students) showed good

13

internal consistency (α = 0.93) and adequate convergent and
discriminant validity. Our current study also showed good
internal consistency for this scale (α = 0.849).
Self-affirmations
The Self-Statements during Public Speaking questionnaire
(SSPS; Hofmann & DiBartolo, 2000) assesses positive and
negative self-statements. It is a 10-item, six-point Likerttype scale, including two subscales. Scores in every subscale range between 5 and 30, with higher scores in every
subscale indicating higher levels of positive or negative
self-statements, respectively. Gallego et al. (2010) validated
the Spanish version in social phobia patients and found
good internal consistency for the positive self-statements
scale (α = 0.81) and for the negative self-statements scale
(α = 0.88). In the current study, the SSPS showed adequate
internal consistency (α = 0.799).
Self-monitoring of intensity, interference of fear, difficulty
and satisfaction
These measures were evaluated through an ad hoc subjective scale with a Likert-type response scale from 1 to 10
(1 = very low, 10 = very high).
Satisfaction and usefulness of the intervention
Global satisfaction with the therapy and usefulness of each
method were anonymously evaluated using a Likert-type
scale from 1 to 10 (1 = very low, 10 = very high).

Procedures
The study was authorized by the Universidad Europea de
Madrid Research Ethics Committee (code CIPI/19/052,
date of approval March 14, 2019). This is also an institutional review board approved study [clinical trials
#NCT05573620]. After being informed about the study,
each patient who provided written informed consent was
assessed to determine eligibility for study entry. Patients
who met eligibility requirements were assessed through a
structured interview and standardized questionnaires and
assigned to a waiting list, IV exposure or VR. The assessment provided specific information to sort topics (health,
culture and arts, equality, education, environmental protection, human relationships, ethical dilemmas) and distractors (people talking, coughing, laughing, yawning, mobile
phone ringing or vibrating, audience asking easy/hard questions, one person standing up) for oral presentations ranging from least to most difficult or troublesome. This allowed
therapists to build a personalized exposure hierarchy for

every participant. Participants assigned to IV or VR arms
received a psychological intervention consisting of a 5-session individual face-to-face ACT-based treatment. VR was
delivered through the Psious platform (currently called
Amelia Virtual Care) distributed in Spain by TEA, using VR
equipment including a Samsung S7 mobile and Samsung
Gear VR glass. The audience in IV exposure was made up
of university students.
The sample size was calculated by the Jamovi jpower
module (Jamovi, 2021). Based on the results of the Wallach et al. (2009) study, which found significant changes in
PSF in the reduction of the social anxiety variable measured
through the LSAS questionnaire with a moderate effect size
(d = 0.635), we would need a sample size of 29 to reliably
(with probability greater than 0.9) detect an effect size of
δ ≥ 0.63, assuming a two-sided criterion for detection that
allows for a maximum Type I error rate of α = 0.05. Details
of the allocated group were given on cards contained in
sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. A therapist researcher enrolled every participant. After acceptance
of a patient, checking inclusion criteria, and obtaining the
patient’s consent, the appropriate numbered envelope was
opened by the therapist researcher in the presence of the
patient; the card inside indicated wether the patient was to
be an IV or a VR case, with immediate or delayed (5 weeks
WL) treatment start. The patient was then assessed, and the
researcher made an appointment for the patient to start intervention. Intervention fidelity was ensured by consistently
monitoring and verifying that the intervention was delivered
according to the established protocol. Fidelity checks were
conducted throughout the study by two external judges, different from the researchers who administered the intervention, who reviewed recordings of the intervention sessions.

Intervention protocol
Intervention protocol was delivered by the first and second
authors and included 5 sessions. Treatment fidelity checklists
were completed by two collaborators who reported 100% of
consistency with the protocol. The structure and content of
the intervention were adapted from a previous pilot study
(Montesinos et al., 2023) and were based on Hayes et al.
(2012) handbook and ACT interventions on PSF (e.g., Brandrick et al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2020), including VR in
the intervention program (Yuen et al., 2019). Session one
took about 90 min and included three parts. Part one focused
on values clarification, aimed at helping the client explore
the meaning of public speaking. It included “the dreamed
professional exercise” (a variation on the “imagine your
funeral” exercise, Hayes et al., 2012). In this exercise, participants were guided to imagine the day of their graduation
at the university and hear from significant people who knew

13

 Current Psychology

about their PSF what they would love to hear on that special
day. This could enlighten them about their dreamed professional. Part two focused on helping the client recognize the
long-term ineffectiveness of avoidance behaviors shown by
functional analysis. Acceptance was then introduced as an
alternative through the “Ship’s captain metaphor” (Harris,
2022). Part three included training in cognitive defusion
(physicalizing exercise, and watching thoughts as graffiti,
a variation on the “soldiers in the parade” exercise; Hayes
et al., 2012). Sessions 2, 3, 4, and 5 lasted one hour and
included again three parts. Part one included more practice
of cognitive defusion exercises after evoking stimuli with
aversive functions (through imagining the imminent oral
presentation context). Additionally, training was provided
to practice approach behaviors to values (e.g., looking at
the therapist’s eyes). Part two included VR or IV exposure
to oral presentation situations in the context of their values.
Part three included feedback and positive reinforcement.
Finally, participants were invited to practice (e.g., ask or
answer questions from the teacher in class) and self-monitoring as homework to promote generalization. Table 1.
shows methods and therapeutic processes in each session.
Instructions for oral presentations in IV and VR conditions
were equivalent. Specifically, in each session from the second to the fifth, participants were asked to improvise a talk
for 12 min about a different topic (e.g., violence against
women, education system, new technologies, cinema and
TV series, climate change…) without notes or PowerPoint.
Participants had 3 min to prepare their speech (access to
the Internet was not allowed). Difficulty progressively
increased based on each participant’s pre-assessment (considering topics and distractors). Participants were assessed
through self-report instruments before and after treatment
and at 3 months follow-up.

Analysis plan
The assumption of homoscedasticity or homogeneity of
variance (Levene’s test) was tested, and Student’s t-test
for independent samples was performed to check the mean
scores of the two groups in pre-intervention for each variable. Differences were verified between the pre-test scores
of the intervention groups. A repeated measures analysis of
variance (ANOVA) was performed between the VR, IV, and
control groups for the pre- and post-treatment measures.
Additionally, a second ANOVA was conducted, incorporating the participants on the WL into each of the intervention
groups (VR vs. IV), and the differences in the pre-treatment,
post-treatment and follow-up scores were analyzed. Post
hoc analyses were used to examine within-group differences
for each of the analyses. The effect size was assessed using
partial eta squared (η2) and Cohen’s d, respectively. Lastly,
the clinical significance of the changes after ACT intervention was evaluated using the method suggested by Jacobson and Truax (1991). The reliable change index (RCI) was
calculated to determine whether the change in participants’
scores was not due to reliability issues. Jacobson and Truax
(1991) proposed three different criteria, each with its own
respective cut-off points. The first criterion, which that best
suits the present study, is a point of two standard deviations
beyond the range of the mean at premeasurement. Subsequently, the process scores in the assessment of anxiety,
interference and satisfaction when speaking in public were
analyzed to verify significant differences between the measures in each of the sessions compared to the initial session.
Finally, the participants’ assessment of the intervention was
descriptively analyzed in terms of usefulness, difficulty and
satisfaction with the therapeutic process.

 Results
Baseline data
The analysis of differences for independent samples in the
pre-test scores between the groups showed no significant
differences in the mean scores between the groups for any
of the variables in the study. Additionally, the normality criterion was met, and the assumption of homoscedasticity of
variance was satisfied for these scores. Since homogeneous
variances are assumed, the parametric analyses presented
below are justified.

Comparison between treatment and control groups
at pre and post-treatment
Table 2 presents the means and standard deviations of the
pre and post scores in the VR, IV intervention groups and
control group. Additionally, the repeated-measures analysis
of variance and post-hoc analysis statistics are included. The
results show statistically significant differences between
groups (group*time interaction) for PSF (PRCS), social
anxiety (LSAS), and self-efficacy (CAHP) and PSF (CIHP)
with a large effect size. Significant differences are found
with a moderate effect size for cognitive fusion (CFQ) and
a small effect size for PI (AAQ-II). Post hoc analyses show
statistically significant differences between pre and post
scores in both the VR and IV intervention groups with a
large effect size for fear of public speaking (PRCS), social
anxiety (LSAS), cognitive fusion (CFQ), and self-efficacy (CAHP) and PSF (CIHP). Furthermore, PI (AAQ-II)
reduces significantly in the IV group with a large effect size.
However, the control group does not report statistically significant differences between pre and post scores for any of
the variables evaluated.

Process measures
Process measures of subjective anxiety intensity, anxiety
interference, and level of satisfaction when speaking in
public were taken throughout the 6 sessions. Figure 2 illustrates the mean scores in each of these variables throughout
the intervention. Firstly, a significant reduction in the intensity of anxiety is observed when speaking in public, with
a large effect size (F (2.67) = 11.54, p < 0.001, η2 = 0.308).
This reduction differs significantly from session 1 from session 4. Additionally, a significant reduction is observed in
the interference scores when speaking in public throughout
the sessions, with statistically significant results and a large
effect size (F (3.30) = 15.68, P < 0.001, η2 = 0.376). Significant differences were found starting from session 3 compared to the initial session. Finally, regarding the assessment
of satisfaction when speaking in public, an increase was
found throughout the sessions, with statistically significant
differences and a large effect size (F (3.10) = 17.01, p < 0.001
η2 = 0.395). No differences were found between the VR and
IV groups.

Clinically significant changes
Once the scores were analysed at a statistical level, the
aim was to assess the range of significant clinical change
(Table 4). To analyse the most powerful effects, we used
first criterion (recovery) proposed by Jacobson and Truax
(1991). Regarding social anxiety (LSAS), the recovery
rate for the VR group was 61.53% at post-treatment, while
69.23% showed recovery at follow-up. For the IV group,
the recovery rate was 92.85% at post-treatment and followup. Concerning PSF (PRCS), the recovery rate for VR participants was 84.61% at post-treatment and follow-up, while
for IV group, recovery rate was 100% at post-treatment and
follow-up.
Regarding PI (AAQ-II), 17.74% of the VR participants
recovered completely at post-treatment, and 29.41% continued to recover at follow-up. For the IV group, 29.41% of
the participants recovered at post-treatment and follow-up.

Qualitative analysis
The degree of general satisfaction with the therapy was 8.9
out of 10, and the usefulness was 8.95. Regarding the degree
of difficulty of the intervention received, an average score

were defusion training, IV or VR exposure, feedback and
positive reinforcement, and being able to talk to the therapist about how they felt.

The application of the intervention was feasible in the university context, well accepted by the participants, and the
majority completed the protocol and showed high adherence. The results suggest that the intervention protocol for
PSF is effective for most of the variables analyzed through
different measurement instruments, with moderate and large
effect sizes. This reflects the contribution of the intervention to reducing PSF, social anxiety, cognitive fusion and
an increasing self-efficacy. Recovery rates for PSF and
social anxiety were very high for both VR and IV conditions. Moreover, ACT-based interventions were more effective than non-intervention in reducing PSF. These outcomes
align with results reported in the scientific literature (Goldfarb, 2009; Kim & Kim, 2012; England et al., 2012; Spencer
et al., 2020; Yuen et al., 2019; Brandrick et al., 2021).

13

 Current Psychology

Regarding the intervention modalities used (IV and VR),
we can conclude that both conditions resulted in decreases
in PSF, social anxiety, and cognitive fusion, as well as
increases in self-efficacy. Although a slight difference in
favor of IV versus VR was observed, we can conclude that
ACT-based exposure through VR is as effective as ACTbased IV exposure, providing more conclusive data than the
pilot studies by Yuen et al. (2019) and in line with the pilot
study by Montesinos et al. (2023).
Although previous studies do not reflect consensus
regarding whether the modification of cognitive contents is
necessary or not to reduce PSF (Taylor, 1996), our study
shows that self-statements were not modified in any of the
intervention modalities, despite clinical significance analysis showing a slight change. This is consistent with ACT
hypotheses, which do not seek to modify the content of the
thoughts but rather to promote defusion and modify the way
of relating to them while orienting actions towards values
(Hayes et al., 2012). The aim is to enhance clinical interactions that allow for full, open and flexible awareness of
the flow of thoughts and emotions to create a more flexible
repertoire (Luciano & Valdivia, 2006). Thus, anxiety and
negative thoughts such as “I can’t”, “they are going to laugh
at me” cease to have a limiting function when carrying out
actions fused or attached to discomfort.
Furthermore, the statistical analysis method proposed by
Jacobson and Truax (1991) allowed an idiographic study
of clinical significant changes. Very high percentages of
recovery were obtained in PSF (assessed through two different measures), social anxiety and self-efficacy. A high
percentage of participants also recovered with respect to PI
and cognitive fusion. Improvements were maintained and
even increased during follow-up, especially in the case of
PSF, where half of the participants continued to recover
three months after completing treatment. These improvement data are consistent with findings in different clinical
problems (Hayes, 2004), affirming the usefulness and effectiveness of ACT in generating substantial changes during
follow-up across a wide range of psychological problems,
thus avoiding chronicity (Luciano & Valdivia, 2006). This
phenomenon is also observed in the PSF (England et al.,
2012). Furthermore, process measures show a decrease in
the interference and subjective intensity of PSF throughout
the training sessions (specially after session 4), highlighting
the importance of persevering in practice when coping with
fears, in line with the improvement in execution and subjective performance reported by Glassman et al. (2016).
Although both treatment modalities were effective, the
study confirmed the advantages specifically mentioned in
the use of VR for the treatment of PSF (Miloff et al., 2016;
Wallach et al., 2009), especially in relation to saving time
and practical benefits by not depending on the collaboration

13

of other people, which, in the case of IV exposure, required
significant effort from the researchers. As in the study by
Botella et al. (2009), students with a high level of PSF
showed high acceptability and willingness to undergo
treatment.
Participants’ verbal reports indicate that the intervention
was effective despite the fact that fear, although reduced,
never completely disappeared, and its intensity remained
moderate or high at the end of the intervention. Interestingly, the change is related to the fact that the PSF began
to fulfil a different function, allowing the context of public speaking to elicit fewer avoidance behaviors over time.
Exposure, whether IV or through VR, is the central component of the intervention and might explain the changes
produced. Unlike exposure delivered in traditional CBT,
habituation or reduction of conditioned anxiety responses is
not intended, nor is exposure directed solely at the external
situation. From the ACT perspective, exposure focuses on
private events and is used to promote PF, training the deliberate choice to remain in the situation in the presence of
discomfort, tuning in to what is important to oneself (Hayes
et al., 2012). In terms of RFT (Hayes et al., 2001), the goal
is a transformation of functions of the “public speaking”
stimulus, where through arbitrary relationships of coordination or causality with “the professional or student who I
want to become”, functions of approaching to private events
related to the PSF are activated, so that the student derives
that “feeling anxiety while speaking in public is part of the
path to learning to effectively communicate”. Likewise, all
the verbal processes belonging to the contained self are put
into perspective through deictic and hierarchical frames
with the private events themselves, so that, in the presence
of these, the student experiences that “I am not my fear” or
“ I am more than my anxiety” and deliberately chooses how
to approach their own values.
An added value of this study compared to previous ones
is the incorporation of a WL control group (England et al.,
2012; Spencer et al., 2020; Yuen et al., 2019), which allowed
a greater degree of control in studying the effectiveness of
the intervention. Another strength of the study is that the
measurement instruments used not only evaluated changes
in emotions (fear), self-statements, and expectations (selfefficacy) but also, from a functional-contextual perspective,
indicators of functional change (cognitive fusion, PI, fear
interference, satisfaction).
Finally, in view of the results of this study, experts and
researchers are encouraged to use VR as the treatment of
choice for PSF when it is difficult to find collaborators available to act as an audience for IV exposure. Therapists are
encouraged to take advantage of the possibilities offered by
VR to individualize, grade, and control the intervention, and
to schedule as many exposure trials as necessary. Therapists

 Current Psychology

are also encouraged to explore the alternative of focusing clients on action and openness to the discomfort that
it entails, rather than on controlling difficult emotions and
negative thoughts.

Limitations
The proposed study is not without limitations. Among
them, it is worth mentioning the small sample size and
its specific demographic structure (predominantly women
educated in health), which limit the generalizability of the
findings. Moreover, since the fieldwork of the clinical trial
was interrupted by the covid-19 pandemic and confinement, some participants were lost due to health problems,
changes in country, or loss of interest due to project delays.
Future research could study this phenomenon using larger
and more representative samples. Additionally, due to limitations in resources for therapist availability and practical
difficulties related to recruitment, the inability to reach the
number of participants estimated for the sample size is also
an important limitation. A larger sample could make the
results more generalizable.
Furthermore, the reliance on self-report measures is a limitation, as bias due to social desirability or recall could affect
the reliability of the results. To address this limitation, our
team is working on analyzing data obtained through behavioral observation from recordings made during training.
Objective anxiety and approach behavioral measures assessed
by external observers could strengthen the validity of the
findings. Future clinical studies might also include another
treatment group different from ACT, based on cognitive control, as has already been done in other works (Brandrick et
al., 2021; Spencer et al., 2020), where differences could be
further explored depending on the theoretical approach.

Conclusion
The results found support the suitability of the psychological flexibility approach in addressing fears in public speaking situations. VR may be successfully combined with ACT
to treat PSF. The effectiveness of exposure is similar when
it is delivered IV compared to VR. The practical advantages
of VR might be considered when therapy is provided in the
university context. Future studies should provide additional
evidence with broader and more diverse samples.

in Psychiatry and Psychotherapy

The effectiveness of acceptance and commitment therapy for
social anxiety disorder: a randomized clinical trial
Samad Khoramnia,1

Amir Bavafa,1 Nasrin Jaberghaderi,1 Aliakbar Parvizifard,1 Aliakbar Foroughi,1
Mojtaba Ahmadi,1 Shahram Amiri1

Abstract
Objective: Acceptance and commitment therapy has been used to treat anxiety disorders recently. The
purpose of this study was to investigate the effectiveness of acceptance and commitment therapy for
psychological symptoms in students with social anxiety disorder, including difficulty in emotion regulation,
psychological flexibility based on experiential avoidance, self-compassion, and external shame.
Methods: This study was a semi-experimental clinical trial. Twenty four students with social anxiety
disorder were randomly divided into two groups after initial evaluations: an experimental group (12
subjects) and a control group (12 subjects). The experimental group received 12 treatment sessions
based on a protocol of acceptance and commitment therapy for anxiety disorders, and the control group
was put on a waiting list. Self-Compassion (SCS), Difficulty in Emotion Regulation (DERS), External
Shame (ESS), Social Anxiety (SPIN), and Acceptance and Action (AAQ-II) questionnaires were used to
assess participants. Data were analyzed using SPSS.
Results: Acceptance and commitment therapy was shown to be effective at the post-test and follow
up stages for reducing external shame, social anxiety, and difficulty in emotion regulation and its
components, and for increasing psychological flexibility and self-compassion (p < 0.05). The largest
effect size of treatment was for increase of psychological flexibility and the lowest efficacy was for the
components “difficulty in impulse control” and “limited access to emotional strategies” at the post-test
and follow-up stages, respectively.
Conclusion: Acceptance and commitment therapy may be an appropriate psychological intervention for
reducing the symptoms of students with social anxiety disorder and helping them to improve psychological
flexibility. Emotion and related problems can be identified as one of the main targets of this treatment.
Clinical trial registration: Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials, IRCT20180421039369N1.
Keywords: Acceptance and commitment therapy, difficulty in emotion regulation, external shame,
psychological flexibility, self-compassion, social anxiety disorder.

Introduction
Social anxiety disorder is characterized by significant
fear or anxiety about one or more social situations in
which the person is exposed to unfamiliar people or to
possible scrutiny by others.1 Social anxiety disorder is one

1

of the most common disorders among young people,2,3
affecting approximately 13% of the population.4 This
disorder, in addition to isolating some patients socially5
and having a destructive effect on occupation and on
educational and interpersonal performance,6 can inflict
huge costs on all countries’ economies every year.7,8

Therefore, comprehensive study of this disorder and
use of evidence-based interventions are important.
Many studies have shown that people with
social anxiety disorder have ineffective experiential
avoidance.9,10 This is related to a person’s desire
for change and sensitivity to internal situations
and events.11 Previous studies have identified selfcompassion,12-15 difficulty in emotion regulation,16-18 and
extreme feelings of shame19,20 as the most important
psychological problems experienced by people with social
anxiety disorder. Clinicians have used pharmacological
and psychological interventions to attempt to improve
the symptoms of social anxiety disorder.21-28 Although
some psychological interventions, such as cognitivebehavioral therapy, have demonstrated efficacy for
treatment of patients with social anxiety, some people
did not respond to treatment or symptoms remained.22
One treatment that has been used recently to treat
anxiety disorders and has demonstrated effectiveness
for reducing anxiety symptoms is acceptance and
commitment therapy (ACT).23-26
ACT is derived from the modern theory of cognition
and language27 and is classified as a third-wave
psychological treatment, in which some cognitivebehavioral therapy concepts have been changed.28
The main assumption underlying ACT is that humans
experience disturbing thoughts, emotions, and
feelings29 and that their attempts to change or to get rid
of these experiences are ineffective, which sometimes
exacerbates these disturbances and ultimately leads
to avoidance.30 The six core psychological processes
employed in this treatment are Acceptance, Defusion,
Self as context, Contact with the present moment,
Values, and Committed action.31 These six processes are
all implemented using metaphors, empirical exercises,
and logical contradictions to escape the literal content
of the language and interact more with the ongoing flow
of experience at the present moment.32 The purpose
of this treatment is to reduce experiential avoidance
and increase psychological flexibility.30 A study by
Azadeh et al.2 demonstrated the efficacy of ACT for the
interpersonal problems and psychological flexibility of
high school girls with social anxiety disorder. In that
study, only clients of one gender were selected and
they were not followed-up to determine the effects
of treatment over time, so the effective and lasting
aspects of the intervention were not evaluated. The
results of a study conducted in 2007 by Dalrymple and
Herbert22 showed that from pre-test to follow-up there
was a significant decrease in symptoms experienced
and improvement in the quality of life of people with
social anxiety after ACT. More studies are needed to
determine the effectiveness of ACT, especially in terms

of cultural differences and variables related to emotion
regulation.
Considering the study of research literature in this
field, as well as the need to study the application of
psychological treatments in different cultures and their
effect on various psychological symptoms, especially
emotion, the importance of further exploration is evident.
The aim of this study is to evaluate the effectiveness
in patients with social anxiety of ACT for psychological
symptoms, including difficulty in emotion regulation,
poor psychological flexibility rooted in experiential
avoidance, self-compassion, and external shame.

Methods
This study was a semi-experimental clinical trial,
with control and experimental groups, that was
approved under code IRCT20180421039369N1 in the
IRCT (Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials). Sampling was
intentional, from among all students with social anxiety
disorder in Kermanshah city. In two recent studies of
the effectiveness of ACT, sample sizes were 19 and
30 individuals.2,22 A sample size of 24 was selected for
the present study. In coordination with the University’s
Counseling Center, posters were put up in college and
dormitory environments and individuals with social
anxiety symptoms were invited to attend a psychological
assessment session. The diagnostic interview was based
on the Anxiety Disorders Interview Schedule for DSMIV (ADIS-IV) and conducted by a clinical psychologist
for all participants.
After reviewing inclusion and exclusion criteria,
individuals willing to participate in the research were
randomly assigned to groups using a random number
generator
(http://stattrek.com/statistics/randomnumber-generator.aspx). Inclusion criteria were as
follows: 1) diagnosis of social anxiety disorder; 2)
informed consent from the patient for participation in
the study; 3) not receiving psychological treatment
during the previous six months; 4) no psychopharmacotherapy during the previous six months;
5) no comorbidity with other anxiety and mood
disorders; 6) absence of other psychiatric disorders
and severe neurological disorders; 7) no substance
abuse or alcohol abuse. Exclusion criteria included
unwillingness to attend continuing treatment sessions
and simultaneous enrollment on another treatment
program. Members of the experimental group attended
twelve 90-minute sessions based on a protocol of ACT
for anxiety disorders.24 Members of the control group
were put on the waiting list. The control group were
given treatment after the final evaluation. A total of

24 students were enrolled on the study, 22 of whom,
in the experimental and control groups, completed the
treatment sessions and pre-test and two-month followup evaluations. One person in the experimental group
was excluded from the study because of unwillingness
to continue attending therapy sessions and one person
in the control group because of non-completion of final
evaluations (Figure 1).
Ethical considerations
In order to comply with ethical standards,
participants were informed of the conditions of the
research and received informed consent forms before
the start of the study. After completing the follow-up
evaluation, individuals in the control group also attended
ACT sessions. After implementation of the protocol, all
research participants were referred to a psychiatrist or
psychologist as necessary for complementary therapies.
This research was approved by the ethics committee
at the Kermanshah University of Medical Sciences (IR.
KUMS.REC.1397.085).

Statistical analysis
SPSS software was used to analyze findings and
statistical data. Multivariate analysis of covariance was
used to analyze the effectiveness of the treatment in
the experimental group on the variables evaluated, in
comparison with the control group. The chi-square test
was used to compare the number of participants and
the independent t test was used to compare the mean
age of the experimental and control groups.
Measurements
Anxiety Disorders Interview Schedule for DSM-IV
(ADIS-IV)
This is a semi-structured, clinical and diagnostic
interview for anxiety disorders developed in 1994 by
Brown et al.33 In addition to anxiety disorders, it also
measures mood disorders, somatization, psychosis,
and drug abuse. The Clinical Severity Rating (CSR) is
scored on a scale from zero (no sign) to eight (severely
disturbed). Accordingly, a severity grading of four or
more indicates that the patient’s symptoms are at or

beyond the diagnostic threshold of the Diagnostic and

Revision (DSM-IV-TR). A degree of severity of three or
below is attributed to diagnoses that are at partial or
full improvement levels. In post-treatment studies using
the ADIS-IV, clinical grade scores are usually used as an
indicator for assessing post-treatment improvement.33
The validity of the Persian version of this program has
been confirmed and its retest reliability coefficient was
reported as 0.83.34 In this study, this measurement will
be used to screen for social anxiety disorder, to confirm
clinical diagnosis, and to assess clinical severity.
Self-Compassion Scale (SCS)
This questionnaire consists of 26 items with a fivepoint Likert response scale measuring three bipolar
components in the form of six sub-scales. These
components are Self-kindness vs. Self-judgment,
Common humanity vs. Isolation, and Mindfulness vs.
Over-identification.35 The Cronbach’s alpha coefficient
of 0.92 represents an internal consistency superior to
the original version of this scale. Convergent validity,
discriminant validity, and appropriate retest reliability
for this scale have been reported.35 In an Iranian
student sample, the six-factor structure of the validation
questionnaire was confirmed and a Cronbach’s alpha
coefficient of 0.86 for the whole scale was reported.
Cronbach’s alpha coefficients for sub-scales were in the
range of 0.79-0.85.35
Difficulty in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS)
This scale is a comprehensive measurement for
assessing difficulty in emotion regulation that is based
on the concept of mindfulness and acceptance and
was designed in 2004.36 A self-report measure with 36
items that measure usual levels of difficulty in emotion
regulation as well as its specific dimensions.37 The scale’s
dimensions are Non-acceptance, Goals lack, Impulse,
Awareness, Strategies, and Clarity.37 Responses are
scored on a five-point Likert scale. The reliability
coefficient for the total scale is 0.93 and the test-retest
is 0.88, while its construct validity is desirable.37 This
scale has been translated into Persian by Khanzadeh et
al. in Iran.38 The subscale validity of this questionnaire
was reported as Cronbach’s alphas between 0.66
and 0.88 and test-retest reliability between 0.97 and
0.91.37,38
External Shame Scale (ESS)
This scale is an 18-item self-report measure,
designed by Gross et al. to measure external shame.39
Each option is scored from “never” to “almost always”
using Likert scales. A higher score indicates greater

external shame.39 The reliability of this measure was
reported as desirable, based on its Cronbach’s alpha
(0.94) and 5-week retest reliability (0.94). This measure
has a moderate correlation with a negative evaluation
of fear and higher correlations with other methods
of measuring shame in clinical student populations.39
Also, this scale has appropriate validity and Cronbach’s
alphas for the whole scale and its related components
have been reported as in the range of 0.71 to 0.93.39
Acceptance and Action in Social Anxiety Questionnaire,
2nd edition (AAQ-II)
This questionnaire was developed to measure the
symptoms of social anxiety or the extent to which
individuals are aware of their thoughts and feelings
about their social anxiety without attempting to change
them.40 ACronbach’s Alpha of 0.94 has been reported
by the scale’s developers.41 The questionnaire also has
good validity.41 The reliability of this questionnaire in
Iran was 0.84 for test-retest and 0.84 for Cronbach’s
alpha and its validity was also desirable.41 The results
of factor analysis by principal component analysis
revealed three components: acceptance, experience
without judgment, and action.40
Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN)
This questionnaire is a self-report scale with 17
items that are designed to assess anxiety or social
anxiety.42 This scale consists of three subscales of
fear (6 items), avoidance (7 items), and physiological
discomfort (4 items), and each item has a 5-degree
Likert response scale, ranging from 1 to 5.42 A cut-off
score of 19 is used to screen for social anxiety. The testretest reliability of this scale has been reported as 0.78
to 0.89 in groups with diagnosed social anxiety and its
internal consistency has been reported as 94% in a
group of healthy individuals.42 The convergent validity
of this questionnaire was reported as 0.57-0.85.42
Intervention
An ACT protocol for anxiety disorders developed by
Eifert and Forsyth24 was used with the intervention group.
This protocol consists of 12 sessions, each with specific
goals. Activities were tailored to the individual needs
of clients, while standard sessions were maintained.
In ACT, emphasis is put on establishment of a context
for acceptance, followed by commitment to values and
action as the main psychological processes. The purpose
of the first session was psycho-education and familiarity
with treatment. In the second and third sessions, the
emphasis was placed on establishing a framework for
acceptance for treatment through evaluation and cost
estimation of past control efforts and creating a space
Trends Psychiatry Psychother. 2020;42(1) – 33

 ACT on students with anxiety - Khorammia et al.

for new solutions, acceptance, or willingness to change.
The fourth and fifth sessions focused on acceptance and
value-based life as an alternative to managing anxiety.
The purpose of the sixth session was to create a pattern
of behavior through value-based exposures. The seventh
to eleventh sessions dealt with commitment to values
and action. In the final session, the treatment sessions
were reviewed and clients were prepared for recurrence
and failure. Various assignments and exercises in
sessions were tailored to the needs of the patients,
such as mindfulness, life-enhancing, and practicing.
The sessions were approximately 90 minutes long.
After the fourth session, one of the clients dropped out
of the treatment sessions and was excluded from the
final evaluations.

Results
Based on demographic variables, the mean age of
the participants was 22.12±1.08. Twenty-four subjects
participated in this study, 17 of whom were women
(70.8%) and 7 of whom were men (29.2%). There
was no significant difference between the two groups
in terms of age (p > 0.05). There was no significant
difference between the two groups in terms of gender
(Table 1). One member of each group was excluded from
the study because of non-completion of the evaluation
and drop-out from treatment sessions respectively.

the control and experimental groups. The table shows

Before statistical inference, the Kolmogorov-Smirnov
test was performed to verify normality of the data and
the data assumption was confirmed. The results of Box’s

multivariate covariance analysis (p > 0.05). The Leven
test was performed to test the equality of error variances
(p > 0.05). Wilk’s Lambda test to measure the efficacy
of the treatment on all target variables showed that the
linear combination of “difficulty in emotion regulation”
and its components was significantly different for control
and experimental groups (Wilk’s Lambda = 0.003, p =

was performed to determine the difference between
the control and experimental groups according to each
target variable.
According to Table 3, the results of multivariate

changes in all therapeutic variables among students
with social anxiety in experimental and control groups
(p < 0.05). In other words, ACT had a significant effect,
reducing external shame, social anxiety, and difficulty
in emotion regulation and its components, while
increasing psychological flexibility and self-compassion

Discussion
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the
effectiveness of ACT for improvement of psychological
symptoms in students with social anxiety disorder.
The psychological symptoms examined were external
shame, psychological flexibility, social anxiety severity,
self-compassion, and difficulty in emotion regulation
and its components. The findings of this study showed
that ACT improved these symptoms in students with
social anxiety disorder in the experimental group,
compared to the control group. The results of a
randomized clinical trial conducted with 73 students
by Yadavaia and colleagues showed that ACT had a
significant effect, increasing self-compassion from
pre-test to follow-up.43 Vowles et al. found that selfcompassion itself could be a powerful mediator of the
effectiveness of ACT, undergoing change under the
influence of treatment.44 Also, the results of this study
showed that the effectiveness of ACT in terms of the
significant increase in students’ self-compassion from
pre-test to follow-up (compared with a control group) is
consistent with previous studies. Although ACT do not
emphasize self-compassion as a target variable, it has
been argued that increased focus on self-compassion in
this treatment may result in a greater effect size for the
effectiveness of ACT.45
Luoma et al.45 showed that ACT is effective for
reducing shame in people with a history of substance
abuse. In another study,46 it was shown that experiential
avoidance can be regarded as a mediator of shame and
self-harmful behaviors. On the other hand, shame can
be a sign and experiential avoidance is a characteristic
experienced by people with social anxiety disorder,9,1921
and experiential avoidance is one of the criteria of
psychological inflexibility in ACT. Therefore, it can be
expected that ACT is effective for reducing feelings of
shame and experiential avoidance, and subsequently
for reducing the self-harmful behaviors of people with
social anxiety disorder, which has been detailed in
several studies.19-21 In line with this conclusion, in the
present study this treatment was effective at reducing
the feelings of shame experienced by students with
social anxiety disorder.
36 – Trends Psychiatry Psychother. 2020;42(1)

One of the main goals of this study was to reduce the
main symptoms of social anxiety disorder in response
to a psychological treatment. Because these symptoms
are debilitating and can have an adverse effect on
individual, social, and occupational health, it is important
to attempt to reduce the symptoms experienced. This
study showed that ACT was effective for reducing the
social anxiety symptoms of the experimental group in
comparison with the control group, as measured by the
Social Phobia Inventory (SPIN). In this study, it was
also shown that this treatment could be effective for
increasing students’ psychological flexibility, which had
the largest effect size of all target variables. In several
other studies, in common with the results of the present
study, ACT has been shown to be effective for reducing
the symptoms of social anxiety disorder.2,47,48 Yadavaia
et al. also showed that ACT is effective for improving
psychological flexibility,43 which is in line with the results
of this study and previous studies.2,49 The explanatory
factors of these results indicate that acceptance and
committed action in ACT can be considered as the
main psychological processes, and it seems that this
treatment, considering the history of research, is
effective for improvement of psychological flexibility
and reduction of symptoms experienced by people with
social anxiety disorder.
The main purpose of this study was to investigate
the effectiveness of ACT at reducing the difficulty
in emotion regulation of people with social anxiety
disorder, which has been shown to be a major concern
in their daily lives.50,51 Of the components of difficulty
in emotion regulation, ACT had the greatest impact on
“lack of acceptance of emotional responses”. In view
of the main psychological processes in this treatment,
this result was not expected. So far, many studies have
been conducted on the effectiveness of psychological
treatments on emotions and related problems.52-54 It
has been argued that ACT emphasizes the experience
of problematic emotions rather than trying to change
knowledge or reduce emotional levels.51 It seems
that ACT is also effective for emotional problems and
changes in levels of emotion. The results presented in
other studies are in line with this.50,51 In the present
study, the results showed that the experimental group
compared favorably to the control group in ability to
effectively reduce the difficulty in emotion regulation
and its components.
Several limitations of this study should be noted. First,
the sample size limits the capability for generalization,
which it is recommended should be addressed in future
studies to increase reliability of results. Second, the
sample studied consisted entirely of students, who are
not comparable with the general population in terms

 ACT on students with anxiety - Khorammia et al.

of social, economic, or intellectual capabilities. Third,
the use of a waiting list group as control group is a
limitation. It is suggested that more dynamic control
groups be used to help clients in future studies.

Conclusion
Given the limitations of this study, it can be concluded
that, by increasing concentration on self-compassion,
ACT can be effective in reducing feelings of shame
and experiential avoidance in students with social
anxiety disorder. This treatment can be an appropriate
psychological intervention to reduce the symptoms
of people with social anxiety disorder and help them
to promote psychological flexibility. According to the
results of this study and the literature on the efficacy of
ACT, emotion and related problems can be identified as
one of the main targets of this treatment.
